notes.setup:
PURPOSE (Sec 1, 3.1): test FineWeb-Edu-style filtering beyond English. An LLM labels data, a small model learns those labels and then filters the pool. They call it MDFS.

LABELLER AND FILTERS: Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct scores about 0.43-0.52M sentences on an additive 5-point prompt (App A, Figs 4-5). Exact counts in Table 5: 464,021 En-De; 520,000 En-Ar quality; 430,260 En-Ar medical; 460,000 En-Ro medical. XLM-R (size not stated) is fine-tuned with a regression head or a 6-way classification head in COMET style, 10 epochs (Sec 4.2, App D, Table 7). For medical only there is also a Moore-Lewis 4-gram KenLM cross-entropy-difference filter, "MDFS-NGRAM" (Sec 3.3). The quality filters see the source and target concatenated (Sec 3.2).

TASK A, TRANSLATION QUALITY (Sec 3.2, 5.1; App C, Table 5):
- En->De: WMT23 ParaCrawl; NMT pool 52,441,859 pairs.
- En->Ar: CCMatrix; pool 30,892,792.
- Kept: the top 1%, 10%, 25% and 50% of the pool by score (Sec 5).
- Baselines: RANDOM, COMET-KIWI (cited as Rei et al. 2022, the CometKiwi WMT22 submission, so CometKiwi-22; checkpoint not named), and full data (dashed line in Fig 1 only).

TASK B, MEDICAL DOMAIN (Sec 3.3, 5.2):
- En->Ar: CCMatrix+UNPC+HLPT+MultiUN+TED; pool 53,971,034.
- En->Ro: CCMatrix+ParaCrawl v9+ELRC-EMEA (783,742); pool 44,739,310.
- They filter on the English side or the non-English side only, and keep 1, 2.5, 5 or 10M sentences.
- Baselines: RANDOM and KEYWORD (30 English keywords, App B Table 6).

PREPROCESSING (App C): all data is near-deduplicated with BiCleaner --aggressive_dedup before the split. They added this after initial En->Ar runs selected many similar sentences.

MT MODEL (Sec 5, App F Table 12):
- From scratch, never fine-tuned. Encoder-decoder Transformer, about 63M parameters, fairseq.
- 100k updates; Adam, lr 5e-4, inverse-sqrt schedule, 4000 warmup; 16k max tokens x update-freq 2; dropout 0.3; label smoothing 0.1.
- Best checkpoint by BLEU on a held-out validation set; beam 5. All directions translate out of English.
- No LLM MT and no fine-tuning arm. The Limitations section names this as a gap.

SEEDS: 3 (42, 2025, 962), reported as mean +- SEM. Random-sampling baselines also redraw the data per seed (App F). 240 NMT models in total (App I).

EVALUATION:
- Quality: FLORES-200, given as a "test set comprising 1,007 sentences" (Sec 5).
- En->Ar medical: TICO-19 (1,000 validation / 2,701 test).
- En->Ro medical: HimL Cochrane (467) + WMT18 biomedical (278).
- Metrics: chrF++ is the main one (they argue neural metrics are less sensitive to named-entity errors, insertions and deletions, Sec 5). spBLEU (sacrebleu) and COMET (wmt22-comet-da) appear in App G.1, Tables 13-16.
- Extras: a gpt-4o-mini pairwise terminology judge on 100 En->Ro sentences (Sec 5.3, App H); learning curves (App G.2 Fig 6); a test set labelled by the LLM (Fig 7).
notes.key_results:
All numbers come from the PDF. Triples are chrF++ / spBLEU / COMET on FLORES-200, mean of 3 seeds.

1. HOW WELL THE FILTERS COPY THE LLM (Sec 4.4, Table 1)
- At threshold 3, every translation-quality filter has F1 >= 0.890.
- At threshold 5, F1 falls to 0.381 (De->En, regression) and 0.398 (En->Ar, regression).
- The authors read this as the filters being unable to tell "good" from "excellent" (Sec 4.4, Conclusion).
- Medical filters (Table 2): F1 at threshold 3 is 0.912-0.976.

2. En->De QUALITY (Table 13)
- 1%: Random 54.7/32.1/0.783; COMET-KIWI 54.8/32.0/0.763; MDFS-Reg 56.5/34.6/0.800; MDFS-Class 56.7/34.7/0.801.
- 10%: Random 59.0/37.8/0.833; COMET-KIWI 61.0/40.8/0.848; MDFS-Reg 60.6/40.3/0.845.
- 25%: Random 59.2/38.0/0.835; COMET-KIWI 61.1/41.0/0.852; MDFS-Reg 60.7/40.4/0.847.
- 50%: Random 59.3/38.3/0.836; COMET-KIWI 60.6/40.3/0.849.
- Sec 5.1: MDFS-Reg at 25% is +1.4 chrF++ over the best Random and +2.8 over full data.

3. En->Ar QUALITY (Table 14)
- 1%: Random 49.7/28.8/0.803; COMET-KIWI 45.2/24.4/0.749; MDFS-Reg 48.3/28.6/0.789; MDFS-Class 48.2/28.5/0.792.
- 10%: Random 55.0/35.2/0.846; COMET-KIWI 54.8/35.0/0.846; MDFS-Class 55.5/36.8/0.854.
- 25%: Random 55.5; COMET-KIWI 55.9; MDFS-Reg 56.2.
- 50%: Random 55.3; COMET-KIWI 56.1; MDFS-Class 56.2.
- Largest MDFS gain over Random for En->Ar: 0.7 chrF++ (Sec 5.1).

4. AUTHORS' SUMMARY (Sec 5.1)
- COMET-KIWI gives worse translations at 1% in both pairs, and at 10% for En->Ar.
- MDFS does better on small selections; COMET-KIWI improves as the selection grows.
- Note: for En->De at 1%, COMET-KIWI ties Random on chrF++/spBLEU and is lower only on COMET (-0.020).

5. MEDICAL DOMAIN (Sec 5.2, Fig 2, Tables 15-16)
- Every MDFS selection beats Random except Romanian MDFS-Reg at 1M: 58.2+-0.5 chrF++ vs Random 58.3; COMET 0.837 vs 0.864.
- En->Ar: MDFS-NGRAM on the Arabic side is strongest, 2.0 chrF++ above Random and 0.4 above the other MDFS models above 1M. Example at 5M: 58.0 vs Random 56.0.
- KEYWORD is competitive at small sizes. At 1M En->Ar, KEYWORD 56.8 = MDFS-Class 56.8.

6. REPETITIVE OUTPUT (Sec 5.2)
- The Romanian MDFS-Reg 1M model produced 68 test outputs that begin "In cazul" followed by a repeated phrase.
- The authors blame unfiltered noisy data amplified by the selection.

7. LEXICAL DIVERSITY, MEDICAL SELECTIONS ONLY (Sec 4.5, Table 4)
- Measure: unique 1-grams in the XLM-R tokenisation of the first 1M tokens of each shuffled 1M-sentence selection, plus median sentence length.
- Arabic pair: Random 19,970 types, median length 27; KEYWORD 14,621 / 37; MDFS variants 12,479-13,900 / 39-46.
- Romanian pair: Random 26,705 / 21; KEYWORD 22,251 / 33; MDFS variants 17,733-21,225 / 35-44.
- My arithmetic: targeted selection has about 27-38% fewer types (Ar) and 17-34% fewer (Ro).
- These narrower sets still beat Random on the in-domain test sets (Tables 15-16).

8. SHARE OF MEDICAL SENTENCES SELECTED (Table 3)
- KEYWORD 4.35% (Ar) / 4.52% (Ro); MDFS-Class 7.12 / 10.54; MDFS-Reg 7.56 / 11.04.

9. LEARNING CURVE (Sec 5.2, App G.2 Fig 6, En->Ro)
- After 5,000 updates, every filter except MDFS-NGRAM (En) matches the best Random chrF++.
- The gap between filtered data and Random shrinks as training goes on.

10. TERMINOLOGY JUDGE (Sec 5.3, Fig 3; En->Ro at 2.5M; 100 sentences; gpt-4o-mini)
- MDFS-Class vs Random: 54% wins vs 18% (28% ties).
- vs KEYWORD: 36% vs 20% (44% ties; the text says "16 percentage points more wins").
- vs MDFS-NGRAM: 26% vs 25% (49% ties).
- These numbers are read from the bar labels in the figure.
notes.their_explanation:
1. FILTER WEAKNESS AT THE TOP. The trained filters reproduce the LLM's coarse good/bad split but cannot rank the very best sentences. Evidence is the low F1 at threshold 5 (Sec 4.4, Conclusion). They never link this causally to MT quality.

2. WHY COMET-KIWI's TOP 1% IS POOR. They give no mechanism, only the description that MDFS suits small selections and COMET-KIWI improves with selection size (Sec 5.1). The language-pair differences between MDFS and COMET-KIWI are "likely" because COMET-KIWI had human DA training data for En-De but not En-Ar (Sec 5.1). This is asserted, not tested.

3. SMALLER En->Ar GAINS. They hypothesise that the CCMatrix pool already holds more high-quality pairs. The only evidence is the comparable chrF++ when training on full data (Sec 5.1).

4. SIMILAR SENTENCES. In initial En->Ar runs, MDFS selected many similar sentences and performance degraded. Their fix was to near-deduplicate all data before any experiment (App C). There are no numbers, no ablation and no explanation. COMET-KIWI is not mentioned in that note.

5. REPETITIVE ROMANIAN OUTPUT. They attribute it to noisy data, because domain filtering does not filter for quality. Selecting a subpopulation risks amplifying biases (Sec 5.2). The evidence is qualitative only.

6. LOWER DIVERSITY OF MEDICAL SELECTIONS. Presented as an expected property of domain filtering (Sec 4.5) and never related to translation quality.

7. SHRINKING BENEFIT WITH LONGER TRAINING. Reported as an observation (App G.2), not explained.
notes.relation_to_C1:
Strict verdict: the paper does not establish C1 and does not contradict it. It partly anticipates the phenomenon, but only as a preprocessing note.

WHY IT CANNOT ESTABLISH C1:
- It never measures repetitiveness (n-gram repetition, duplicate rate) of any selection it scores, CometKiwi or otherwise.
- Source mix is not a variable in the quality experiments: each pool is one corpus (ParaCrawl for En-De, CCMatrix for En-Ar). It therefore cannot separate repetitiveness from source mix.
- It uses one test set per quality experiment (FLORES), with no in-domain vs out-of-domain contrast.
- It trains from scratch for 100k updates and never fine-tunes a converged model.

WHAT IT ANTICIPATES:
- (a) App C reports, anecdotally, that a quality-based filter (their LLM-label filter, En->Ar, initial runs) selected many similar sentences and that this degraded performance. Their response was to near-deduplicate the whole pool. So the idea that quality selection pulls in redundant text, and that this hurts, is in print. It is unquantified, about MDFS rather than CometKiwi, and treated as a nuisance.
- (b) Tables 13-14 show CometKiwi's top 1% is no better than random on chrF++ for En->De (54.8 vs 54.7) but lower on COMET (0.763 vs 0.783), and clearly below random for En->Ar (45.2 vs 49.7 chrF++; 0.749 vs 0.803 COMET).
- That fits C1's premise that the extreme QE tail makes a poor training set. But it was measured after near-dedup, with no diagnosis, and the authors frame it as COMET-KIWI scaling with selection size.

WHAT IS LEFT FOR US: quantifying repetition inside the CometKiwi top band, the controlled within-UN contrast (E0.5), and the fine-tuning regime. All of this is new relative to the paper.
notes.relation_to_C2:
The paper leaves C2 open: it neither establishes nor contradicts it.

(a) CometKiwi's top 1% still lost to random after near-deduplication.
- En->Ar: -4.5 chrF++, -4.4 spBLEU, -0.054 COMET (Table 14).
- En->De: -0.020 COMET (Table 13).
- This loosely supports "the top band is worse than random even without duplication".
- But BiCleaner near-dedup is not our rep = 0 criterion (no 8-gram repeated within the band).
- They computed no diversity statistic for these QE selections.
- They offer a competing account: language-pair coverage in COMET-KIWI's training (Sec 5.1).

(b) Table 4 is the only vocabulary evidence, and it covers medical selections only.
- Targeted selections cut distinct unigrams by about 27-38% (Ar) and 17-34% (Ro) against random (my arithmetic from Table 4), and lengthen sentences.
- Yet the same selections beat random on in-domain tests (Tables 15-16). Their models are never evaluated out of domain.
- So in their setting, narrow vocabulary coexists with gains and is not shown to cause harm.
- They never manipulate vocabulary and never test it as a cause.

Implication for C2: narrow vocabulary alone cannot carry the argument, since a reviewer can point to Table 4. What separates our case is that our diverse half also hurts in-domain (UN test -2.11 vs baseline, while random UN gives +0.20). That is not the "focused but helpful" pattern of their domain selections.
notes.how_to_position:
Suggested Related Work text:

"Waldendorf et al. (2025) compare CometKiwi with filters trained on LLM labels for from-scratch NMT. CometKiwi's top 1% is no better than random selection for En-De and clearly worse for En-Ar. They also note in passing that quality filters select many similar sentences, which they remove by near-deduplication. We isolate and quantify this effect in fine-tuning: inside the CometKiwi top band, repetitive text costs 2.6 BLEU against non-repetitive text when source, length and score are matched, and a smaller gap to random data remains even without repetition."
notes.reviewer_risk:
1. "ALREADY KNOWN; JUST DEDUPLICATE." A reviewer can say Waldendorf et al. (2025, App C) already saw quality filters select many similar sentences that hurt performance, and treat near-dedup (BiCleaner --aggressive_dedup) as routine, so C1 is a deduplication artefact.
- Our defence: our "repetitive" label is 8-gram repetition within the band, not only duplicates (the exact duplicate rate is 8.45%).
- We still need a run showing the repetitive-vs-diverse gap survives standard near-dedup of the band or pool. Without it, this objection is strong.

2. "QE SELECTION HELPS IN THEIR EXPERIMENTS." In Table 13 (En->De, from scratch), CometKiwi's top 10-50% beats random by 1.3-2.0 chrF++ and 2.0-3.0 spBLEU. A reviewer may argue our damage is specific to fine-tuning a converged model, to UN-heavy En-Fr, or to the extreme tail.
- We must state that our band is the top ~6% of the pool, in a fine-tuning regime.
- Their own top-1% results (En->Ar -4.5 chrF++; En->De -0.020 COMET) actually support a tail problem, so we can cite them for that.

3. "IT IS QE MISCALIBRATION." They attribute pair-dependent COMET-KIWI behaviour to whether the pair was in its human DA training data (Sec 5.1). A reviewer could say our top band reflects CometKiwi miscalibration on En-Fr UN text rather than repetitiveness. E0.5 matches QE score within UN text, which partly answers this.

4. AGAINST C2: "NARROW VOCABULARY IS NORMAL." Table 4 shows lower lexical diversity in selections that still improve in-domain translation, so narrowness is a generic signature of selection and not harmful in itself.

5. SMALLER POINTS: their learning-curve result (filtering benefits shrink with more updates, App G.2) invites the question of whether our 10k-step gap is stable over training. They also use 3 seeds and redraw random data per seed; check that our random arm does the same.

notes.author_must_check:
1. The CometKiwi checkpoint is not named. The paper cites Rei et al. 2022 (the CometKiwi WMT22 submission). Confirm it matches our CometKiwi-22 before calling it "the same scorer".

2. XLM-R model size is never stated.

3. App C says they "deduplicate all data". The note sits after an En->Ar remark, but the wording suggests it covers every setup, En->De included. Confirm before claiming their CometKiwi results come from deduplicated pools.

4. Which side COMET-KIWI scored (always En->X?) is not stated.

5. FLORES-200 is described as a "test set comprising 1,007 sentences" with no split named. I did not verify that figure.

6. Table 4 does not say which side is tokenised (English or non-English), only that the XLM-R tokeniser is used on the first 1M tokens of the shuffled 1M-sentence selection.

7. Numbers from my own arithmetic or read off figures:
- Selection sizes: 1% is about 524k pairs for En->De and about 309k for En->Ar.
- The 17-38% type reductions.
- The Fig 3 win rates (from bar labels).
- The full-data En->De chrF++ (about 57.9), inferred from the stated "+2.8"; the dashed full-data line has no table values.

8. Sec 5.1 says COMET-KIWI gives "worse translations at 1%" for both pairs. For En->De that holds only against MDFS and on COMET: chrF++ 54.8 vs Random 54.7, spBLEU 32.0 vs 32.1. Do not cite it as "below random on chrF++" for En->De.

9. Their explanation for COMET-KIWI's pair dependence is that it lacked En-Ar human DA training data. Check CometKiwi-22's DA training coverage for En-Fr and En-De before a reviewer uses that argument against us.

10. This paper did not test whether our in-band repetition effect survives BiCleaner aggressive near-dedup. We have to run that ourselves.
notes.useful_for_design:
EN-DE REPLICATION
- Their En->De pool (WMT23 ParaCrawl, 52.4M) with CometKiwi top-k is a direct reference point.
- Their top 10-50% beats random, while the top 1% only ties random on chrF++ and loses on COMET (Table 13). Report where our band sits (fraction of pool) and, if affordable, add one larger fraction, so we show the harm is a tail effect and do not contradict them.
- Evaluate on FLORES-200 as well, with chrF++ and COMET (wmt22-comet-da) next to BLEU, so the numbers are comparable.
- Add a near-dedup control: run BiCleaner --aggressive_dedup (their exact tool and flag, App C) on the pool or band, then recompute rep and rerun repetitive vs diverse. This answers the "just deduplicate" objection directly.

LLM / LoRA ARM
- Their Limitations section says they only trained small models from scratch and did not fine-tune larger multilingual models. Our fine-tuning and LoRA arms fill exactly that gap; cite it that way.
- Their learning curves (App G.2) show filtering effects shrink with more updates. Log intermediate checkpoints in both the NMT and LoRA arms to show our gap is not transient.

VOCABULARY EXPERIMENT
- Add their diversity measure as a second one: distinct subword 1-grams (XLM-R tokeniser) within a fixed token budget (first 1M tokens of a shuffled selection), with median length alongside (Table 4). Our "word types at identical word counts" follows the same logic; reporting both lets reviewers compare.
- Their Table 4 / Fig 2 pattern (narrow vocabulary but in-domain gains) means the vocabulary test must keep the in-domain UN test. That separates focusing that helps from narrowness that hurts.
- Design the manipulation to change vocabulary while holding domain, length and QE score fixed. Their Moore-Lewis n-gram LM cross-entropy scoring (KenLM 4-gram, Sec 3.3) is a cheap tool for building matched selections.

SEEDS AND BASELINES
- They redraw the random data per seed (App F). Confirm our random-UN arm does the same.

notes.setup:
TASK FRAMING: this is a data-pruning paper. Its main contribution is a new selector, CAT. QE is one of several baselines, not the subject of the paper.

LANGUAGE PAIRS / DATA (Sec 4.1): three pairs, all out of English.
- en-de: WMT19, 38M pairs.
- en-fr: WMT15, about 38M pairs.
- en-sw: WMT22, 22M web pairs aligned with LASER. Table 3 gives about 23M.
Because of compute limits, most experiments run on a random 3.8M-pair subset of each corpus. That is 10% of de/fr and 17% of sw.
"Full-scale" runs on the whole corpora (Sec 5.5, Table 3) cover only CAT-DIFF(1,5), LaBSE and Random, at a 90% prune level.

WHAT IS KEPT (Sec 4.3, Sec 3):
- Prune levels are 50%, 70% and 90%, so the kept share is 50%, 30% or 10% of the sentences.
- Budgets are matched on sentence count. Token count is not matched.
- CAT-DIFF (Sec 3.1):
  - Train an NMT model on the full set for a few epochs.
  - Compute per-sentence perplexity at epoch 1 and at epoch k (k = 5 or 2).
  - Rank sentences by the perplexity drop PPL_1 - PPL_k and keep those above a percentile.
- CAT-VAR (Sec 3.2): take the variance of perplexity across epochs 1, 3 and 5, and keep a band around the median.
- Baselines (Sec 4.4):
  - Random selection.
  - COMET-QE (cited as Rei et al., 2020; the exact checkpoint is not named).
  - LaBSE and LASER embedding similarity.
  - Target-side perplexity under BLOOM 560M, 1.1B and 1.7B.
  - Sec 4.4 calls the embedding and QE methods together "Translation Quality Estimators".
- The paper does not say explicitly that COMET-QE, LaBSE and LASER keep the highest-scoring pairs. That is the natural reading.
- COMET-QE is reported only for en-de and en-sw at 3.8M (Tables 4-5). It is NOT run for en-fr (Table 6 has only CAT-DIFF, Random and LaBSE) and is not run at full scale.

QE METRIC: COMET-QE (WMT20-era, Rei et al. 2020), not CometKiwi.

MODEL (Sec 4.3, Table 1):
- Every subset is used to train a model FROM SCRATCH. There is no fine-tuning and no LLM translator.
- fairseq "vanilla transformer" with GeLU. Base or big size is not stated.
- Adam (0.9, 0.98), lr 5e-4, inverse-sqrt schedule, 4,000 warmup steps, label smoothing 0.1, dropout 0.2.
- Effective batch 16K, FP16, at most 30 epochs, max length 256.
- Separate 16K SentencePiece vocabularies for source and target, trained on the 3.8M pairs.
- Hardware: 4x A100 40GB. Runs take about 1, 2, 3 and 4.5 h at 90%, 70%, 50% and full, so smaller subsets get fewer updates.
- BLOOM is used only as a scorer, never fine-tuned.

SEEDS:
- Figure 4 caption: the error bars on the German and French plots are min/max BLEU over 5 runs "with different random seeds for data selection".
- It is unclear which methods this covers, or whether model initialisation seeds vary.
- The +/- values in Tables 4-6 appear to be paired-bootstrap intervals (Appendix B: 1000 resamples, Koehn 2004), not seed spread.

EVALUATION (Sec 4.2, 4.3, App. B):
- en-de: WMT18 newstest (2,998 sentences) and FLORES.
- en-fr: WMT15 newstest (1,500 sentences) and FLORES.
- en-sw: FLORES (1,012 sentences, WikiNews/WikiJunior/WikiVoyage) and MAFAND-MT (1,835 news sentences).
- Metrics: SacreBLEU (signature nrefs:1|case:mixed|eff:no|tok:13a|smooth:exp|version:2.3.2, footnote 3), plus chrF++ and COMET in the appendix. The COMET model is not named ("default configurations").
- There is no in-domain test set matched to the training-data sources.
notes.key_results:
All numbers are from the 3.8M-pair setting unless marked otherwise. Format is BLEU on FLORES / second test set.

1) en-de, COMET-QE selection vs Random (Table 5, BLEU)
   - 90% prune (keep top 10%): COMET-QE 16.7 / 19.4 (WMT18) vs Random 23.7 / 28.6 vs Full 31.5 / 38.8.
   - 70% prune: COMET-QE 28.5 / 33.9 vs Random 28.8 / 34.9.
   - 50% prune: COMET-QE 30.7 / 37.8 vs Random 30.0 / 36.7.

   - Sec 5.2 states that random beats the "translation quality estimators" at 90% and 70% on both German test sets.

   - en-sw FLORES: 29.3, 33.6, 20.3, 33.0.
   - en-sw MAFAND: 24.5, 28.9, 15.3, 27.5.
   For Swahili, CAT-DIFF falls far below random at full scale, although it beat random at 3.8M (25.0 vs 15.7 FLORES, Table 4). Sec 5.5 nevertheless calls the results "similar".

7) Headline efficiency claims
   - Sec 5.4: CAT-DIFF(1,5) keeps 99% of full-data German performance at 50% prune.
   - Fig. 4 caption: above 77% of full at 90% prune and above 92% at 50% prune for de/fr.
   - Table 2: CAT-DIFF(1,5) beats CAT-DIFF(1,2) in most cells.

8) Analysis (Sec 6, Figs. 5-6), descriptive only
   - Longer target sentences correlate with higher BLEU for de and fr, and CAT-DIFF favours longer sentences (Fig. 5).
   - CAT-DIFF selects more unique and rare words and a lower mean word frequency for de and sw.
   - For fr, LaBSE favours unique and rare words (Fig. 6 caption).
   - The exact Fig. 6 counts cannot be read from the PDF text. The axes run roughly 300k-800k unique words.
   - COMET-QE's selection is NOT included in this lexical analysis.
   - Appendix A (Figs. 7-8): the de and fr 3.8M samples contain length outliers (some sentences of 500+ words) and foreign-language text. The sw sample does not.
notes.their_explanation:
Why CAT works:
- Sec 1 hypothesises that sentences whose perplexity changes most between early checkpoints are "easy" examples that the model learns fastest.
- Sec 6 reports, descriptively, that CAT-DIFF picks longer sentences and more unique and rare words.
- They say its choices are "far more complex than selecting the longest sentences". For Swahili, taking the longest sentences does not raise BLEU.
- A deeper look is left to future work. No intervention tests the length or lexical-diversity explanation, and lexical counts are not normalised for the extra tokens that longer sentences bring.

Why the QE and embedding selectors fail on German but work on Swahili:
- Sec 5.2 attributes this to differences in data quality between the two corpora.
- The German data has high sentence-length variance and foreign-language content.
- The Swahili data is already processed, automatically aligned, low in length variance and free of foreign-language text (App. A, Figs. 7-8).
- So "selecting the best sentences" helps when the pool is mined bitext.
- This is supported only by those descriptive plots. Nobody filters the German data and re-runs QE selection. Nobody examines what COMET-QE or LaBSE actually picked in German, for example duplicates, short sentences, copies or a single dominant source.
- The paper never discusses repetition, duplication or domain/source make-up of the selected subsets.

Why the LLM-perplexity selectors work for Swahili but not German:
- Sec 5.3 only suggests that pretrained LLMs can help when data and compute are both scarce. This is not tested.
notes.relation_to_C1:
LEAVES C1 OPEN. It neither establishes nor contradicts it. It does independently document the phenomenon that C1 tries to explain.

What it does show:
- In en-de (3.8M WMT19 sample, models trained from scratch), keeping the top 10% by COMET-QE scores far below random: 16.7 vs 23.7 FLORES and 19.4 vs 28.6 WMT18 (Table 5).
- Top 10% is close to our top band's share of the pool: about 1M of 16.6M, roughly 6%.
- The deficit almost disappears when 30% is kept and reverses slightly when 50% is kept (Table 5).

What it does not do:
- It never measures repetition, n-gram reuse, duplicate rate or the source/domain make-up of the QE-selected subset.
- Its only lexical analysis (Fig. 6) leaves COMET-QE out.
- Its explanation for QE's weakness is noise in the pool: length outliers and foreign-language text (Sec 5.2, App. A). That is a different mechanism from repetitiveness and is not tested either.
- The setting also differs from ours in four ways:
  - training from scratch, not fine-tuning a converged model;
  - COMET-QE 2020, not CometKiwi-22;
  - no en-fr QE arm at all (Table 6);
  - the budget is matched on sentence count, not on length.
- So it gives no evidence on whether repetitiveness or source mix drives the damage.

It only supports C1's premise that QE top-band selection can be harmful in a high-resource pair. Note that in Swahili, mined bitext, COMET-QE was roughly equal to or better than random (Table 4).
notes.relation_to_C2:
LEAVES C2 OPEN. There is weak correlational support and one possible counter-example.

Support:
- The best-performing selector in de and sw (CAT-DIFF) picks more unique and rare words and a lower mean word frequency (Sec 6, Fig. 6).
- This fits the idea that lexical breadth matters.

Why it cannot be cited as evidence for C2:
(a) Lexical counts come from subsets matched on sentence count. CAT-DIFF favours longer sentences (Fig. 5), so more unique words may just reflect more tokens. Nothing is normalised to equal word counts, as our 33,874 vs 58,441 types comparison is.
(b) COMET-QE's subsets are not analysed lexically, so the paper says nothing about whether QE-selected data is lexically narrow.
(c) No experiment manipulates vocabulary.
(d) No condition removes repetition while holding QE score fixed, which is the comparison C2 depends on.

Possible counter-example in our own pair:
- For en-fr, Fig. 6's caption says LaBSE favours unique and rare words.
- Yet LaBSE is the WORST en-fr selector at 90% prune: 31.4 / 25.1 vs Random 32.9 / 26.9 and CAT 33.5 / 28.2 (Table 6).
- The caption itself concludes that the selectors follow no uniform lexical pattern across languages.
- So in their data, more vocabulary does not reliably mean better BLEU.
- This rests on the caption. The exact French values cannot be read from the figure in text form.
notes.how_to_position: Chimoto et al. (2024) find that training en-de Transformers from scratch on the top 10% of a WMT19 sample ranked by COMET-QE gives far lower BLEU than a random 10%. They attribute QE's weakness to a noisy, heterogeneous high-resource pool, but do not look at what the QE-selected subset contains. We study that subset directly in a fine-tuning setting. With length, source and QE score controlled, its repetitiveness accounts for most of the out-of-domain loss, and even its non-repetitive half stays below random data.
notes.reviewer_risk:
1) NOVELTY OF THE PHENOMENON
"That QE-ranked top subsets underperform random selection in a high-resource pair was already shown by Chimoto et al. (2024, Table 5)."
- Defence: they establish the phenomenon (from scratch, COMET-QE, en-de) but not the cause.
- Our contribution has to be framed as the mechanism, not the observation. This matches the memory note that the phenomenon is pre-empted.

2) RIVAL MECHANISM
"Chimoto et al. attribute QE failures to pool noise (length outliers, foreign-language text; Sec 5.2, App. A). Did you rule that out before blaming repetitiveness?"
- Our halves are length-matched and QE-matched.
- I have no evidence here that we compared language-ID contamination or length-ratio outliers between the repetitive and diverse halves. If we did not, a reviewer can raise it.

3) C2 AND LEXICAL DIVERSITY
"Their en-fr analysis has the more lexically diverse selector (LaBSE) doing worse (Table 6, Fig. 6 caption), and they find no uniform lexical pattern. Why should vocabulary narrowness explain your residual gap?"
- This makes it risky to present vocabulary as more than a hypothesis.

4) BAND SIZE DEPENDENCE
"In their en-de results the QE deficit disappears once 30-50% is kept (Table 5). Is your effect an artefact of the very narrow top ~6% band?"
- They will want at least one larger band.

5) METRIC CHOICE
"Their COMET-QE-selected en-de model ranks first on COMET at 50% prune but not on BLEU (Table 5). Your conclusions are BLEU-only."
- If we add COMET, the reviewer may also point out that CometKiwi-selected data evaluated with COMET shares a metric family.

6) SCALE FRAGILITY
"Their Swahili ranking reverses between 3.8M and full scale (Table 4 vs Table 3). Does your finding hold at other pool sizes?"
- Note that this reversal involves CAT-DIFF, not QE.

notes.author_must_check:
Please check these against the PDF before citing.

2) Meaning of "+/-". The +/- values in Tables 4-6 look like paired-bootstrap intervals, not seed spread. They are not labelled.

3) Seeds. The 5-seed error bars (Fig. 4 caption) cover German and French only, and only "random seeds for data selection". It is unclear whether this applies to every method or to model initialisation.

4) Selection direction. The paper never says explicitly that COMET-QE, LaBSE and LASER keep the TOP-scoring pairs. I assumed so. For BLOOM, Sec 4.4 suggests that easy and hard examples sit on the tails, so a middle band may have been kept. This is ambiguous.

5) Model names. Neither the exact COMET-QE checkpoint (only "Rei et al., 2020") nor the COMET evaluation model ("default configurations") is named.

6) Figures without numbers.

   - Figure 6 lexical values (unique words, rare words, mean frequency) cannot be read from the text.

7) Internal inconsistencies in the paper.

   b) Sec 5.5 calls the full-scale results "similar" to 3.8M, but Swahili CAT-DIFF flips from far above random (Table 4) to far below it (Table 3).

   d) The Limitations sentence about running only "German and English" at scale looks garbled.

8) Model size. Transformer size (base vs big) is not stated. Do not describe their model as Transformer-base.

9) Possible link to repetition (my speculation only). The LaBSE collapse in German (5.4 / 7.5 BLEU at 90%; 9.2 / 6.4 at full scale) is extreme and goes unexplained. It may reflect degenerate or duplicate top-scored pairs, which would bear on our repetitiveness story. Do not cite it as evidence.
notes.useful_for_design:
EN-DE REPLICATION

1) Clean the pool first. Their WMT19 en-de sample had length outliers and foreign-language text (App. A), and they blame QE's failure on exactly that.
   - Before comparing the repetitive and diverse halves, run language ID and source/target length-ratio filters on the whole pool, or at least report contamination rates per half.
   - This pre-empts their rival explanation.

2) Run at least two band sizes. Their QE deficit is large only when 10% is kept and disappears at 30-50% (Table 5).
   - For example, the top ~6% plus a wider band.
   - This shows whether repetitiveness still predicts damage as the band widens.

3) Add FLORES as a second out-of-domain test next to newstest. Their en-de/en-fr results use newstest plus FLORES, which makes our numbers directly comparable.

4) Fix and report the BLEU setup. Use their signature (tok 13a, sacreBLEU 2.x) or report ours explicitly. Also report chrF++ and paired-bootstrap tests, as they do (App. B).

METRICS AND BUDGET

5) If you add COMET:
   - Their COMET-QE selection ranks higher on COMET than on BLEU (Table 5, 50% prune).
   - Report a non-COMET-family metric alongside, or state the selection/evaluation overlap as a caveat.

6) Budget matching is our strength. They match on sentence count, while selectors that favour longer sentences get more tokens per epoch, and smaller subsets get fewer updates (30-epoch cap, 1-4.5 h runs).
   - Our length-matched, fixed-step design avoids both problems.
   - Say so explicitly. It also fits the compute-alignment angle.

VOCABULARY EXPERIMENT

7) Normalise everything to equal token counts. Fig. 6 does not, so its diversity counts are confounded with length.
   - Report their three statistics, all at equal token count:
     - unique word types;
     - "rare words" (define the frequency threshold against the 16.6M pool);
     - mean word frequency.
   - Their statistics then become directly comparable to ours.

8) Design the test so it can fail. Their French evidence (LaBSE more diverse but worse) is a ready counter-example.
   - Vary vocabulary breadth while holding length, QE score, source mix and repetition fixed. One option is subsampling the diverse half to match the random-UN type count, or the reverse.
   - This is a test that a "more types = better" prediction could fail.

9) Subword vocabulary. Their 16K SentencePiece vocabularies are trained on the full sample.
   - In our fine-tuning setup the subword vocabulary is fixed by pretraining.
   - Consider also reporting subword-type coverage, not only word types, since rare words split into known pieces.

LLM LoRA ARM

10) Little direct guidance. BLOOM appears only as a perplexity scorer (worse than random for de, about random or slightly better for sw; Table 5 / Table 4), never as a fine-tuned translator.
   - The paper offers no precedent for LoRA fine-tuning on QE-selected data, so that arm is not pre-empted here.

notes.setup:
- Paper type: the University of Amsterdam team's WMT24 general-task system description. The QE experiments are side experiments inside it.
- Language pairs: QE filtering of NMT training data covers en->zh, en->ja and ja->zh. LLM fine-tuning and post-editing are en->zh only (Sec 1 footnote 1; Sec 4.1).
- Data: all WMT24 constrained-track data. Table 1 counts, raw -> cleaned -> QE-filtered:
  - en->zh: 55,346,004 -> 39,354,051 -> 22,606,804
  - en->ja: 33,875,162 -> 26,415,631 -> 14,507,351
  - ja->zh: 22,642,553 -> 12,560,471 -> 6,679,265
- Cleaning (Sec 2): Moses scripts (at most 256 tokens; source/target token ratio at most 3; drop pairs with more than 75% identical words; exact dedup); FastText language ID; drop one-to-many and many-to-one mappings. The paper does not list which corpora the pool contains or how much each contributes.
- QE metric: "the COMETKiwi model" (Sec 3.1). The version wmt22-cometkiwi-da is named only for the post-editing selector (Sec 3.3), and the introduction calls the tool "COMET". Scores are on a 0-100 scale.
- What is kept, NMT: a threshold that drops everything below 80 (en->zh, en->ja) or below 65 (ja->zh) (Sec 3.1). From Table 1, that keeps about 57%, 55% and 53% of the cleaned data. This removes roughly the bottom half; it is not top-k selection.
- What is kept, LLM (Sec 5.2, Table 4): all 39M cleaned en->zh pairs were scored, and these fine-tuning sets were built:
  - 10k and 100k "Cleaned" (described as random samples in the caption)
  - all 53k pairs with COMET > 89 (about 0.13% of the pool)
  - 53k, 100k and 300k pairs with COMET > 87 (300k is about 0.76% of the pool)
- NMT model: multilingual Transformer-large (12 layers, 16 heads, d=1024, dff=4096, 419M parameters, pre-norm, tied embeddings) trained from scratch on all directions in fairseq. Settings: lr 5e-4, inverse-sqrt schedule, 4k warmup steps, FP16, 4x A6000, early stopping with patience 5. It is then fine-tuned on each direction's own subset (Sec 3.1, 4.1). "mT-large + QE" is retrained from scratch on the QE-filtered data.
- LLM: LLaMA2-7B fine-tuned with the ALMA framework, skipping ALMA's monolingual stage. Batch 32, gradient accumulation 4, lr 2e-5, 1 epoch, bf16, beam 5 (Sec 3.2). The paper does not say whether this is full fine-tuning or LoRA.
- Post-editing uses Tower-Instruct 7B/13B without training.
- Seeds: none reported. Every number appears to be a single run, with no variance or significance tests.
- Evaluation (Sec 4.2-4.3): FLORES-200 devtest, NTREX, and the WMT24 official test set (BLEU/ChrF from the OCELoT submission system). Earlier WMT sets serve as validation. Metrics: SacreBLEU (signature tok:13a), ChrF++, COMET wmt22-comet-da.
- Table 4, the QE-subset LLM experiment, reports only FLORES devtest BLEU and COMET.

1. **Removing low-QE pairs helps NMT trained from scratch** (Sec 5.1; Tables 2 and 3):
   - en->zh, mT-large -> +QE (Table 3, rows 1-2): FLORES BLEU 42.2 -> 43.8 (+1.6), ChrF 35.0 -> 36.0, COMET 84.94 -> 86.21. NTREX BLEU 33.3 -> 34.7 (+1.4), COMET 79.20 -> 81.21.
   - en->ja (Table 2, rows 1-2): WMT24 BLEU 29.8 -> 34.2 (+4.4); FLORES 35.9 -> 36.6; NTREX 26.9 -> 27.3.
   - ja->zh (Table 2, rows 4-5): WMT24 BLEU 22.5 -> 22.7 (+0.2); FLORES BLEU 33.9 -> 34.0 but ChrF 29.2 -> 29.1.
   - Per-direction fine-tuning adds little: en->zh FLORES 43.9, NTREX 35.0, WMT24 BLEU 33.5 (Table 3, row 3).
2. **LLaMA2-7B en->zh, FLORES devtest, BLEU / COMET** (Table 4; Sec 5.2):

   | Fine-tuning set | BLEU | COMET |
   |---|---|---|
   | 10k Cleaned | 28.0 | 82.7 |
   | 100k Cleaned | 35.7 | 85.6 |
   | 53k COMET>87 | 36.1 | 86.1 |
   | 53k COMET>89 (all such pairs) | 33.5 | 84.3 |
   | 100k COMET>87 | 35.5 | 85.7 |
   | 300k COMET>87 | 34.6 | 86.6 |

   - Same size, top slice vs slightly lower slice: >89 is 2.6 BLEU and 1.8 COMET below >87 (my subtraction).
   - Top band vs Cleaned at 100k: 35.5 vs 35.7 BLEU and 85.7 vs 85.6 COMET. Selecting by QE gives no gain.
   - More top-band data, 100k -> 300k at >87: BLEU 35.5 -> 34.6, while COMET rises 85.7 -> 86.6.
   - Size matters most: 10k -> 100k Cleaned is +7.7 BLEU.
3. **The 300k >87 LLaMA2 has the highest FLORES COMET but lags on BLEU** (Table 3, row 4; Sec 5.2): COMET 86.60, but 7.6 BLEU and 3.8 ChrF below mT-large. Those deltas match row 1, not row 3.
4. **Post-editing** (Table 3, rows 7-9; Sec 5.3): PED(3+5) beats the NMT system on WMT24 by +4.6 BLEU and +3.3 ChrF (38.1/34.9 vs 33.5/31.6). QE-based PED reaches 38.2/35.3. Post-editing hurts on FLORES and NTREX. Not relevant to our claims.
notes.their_explanation:
- **NMT gain:** they credit removing misaligned or noisy web-crawled pairs, wrong-language text and non-linguistic content (motivation in Sec 3.1, citing Khayrallah & Koehn 2018, Kreutzer et al. 2022 and Peter et al. 2023). They do not test this beyond the before/after scores and do not look at what was removed.
- **LLM results:** they offer no reason why the >89 slice is worse, or why >87 does no better than Cleaned. Their only takeaway (Sec 5.2, paraphrased): raising fine-tuning data quality as COMET measures it is not a promising approach for LLMs, while data size matters.
- **Never measured:** source-corpus mix, domain, length, duplicates, repetitiveness or vocabulary of any QE slice. There are no seeds and no second test set for Table 4. The result is an observation without a tested mechanism.
notes.relation_to_C1:
**Leaves C1 open.** It neither supports nor contradicts it. It does already report the general effect, top-QE selection hurting fine-tuning, in a different setting.

- **Setting differs:**
  - Theirs: LLaMA2-7B fine-tuned on en->zh, one run, FLORES devtest only, 53k pairs above 89 (about 0.13% of a 39M pool).
  - Ours: a from-scratch Transformer-base fine-tuned on en->fr, about 1M pairs (about 6% of 16.6M), 5 seeds.
- **Different comparison:** their contrast is the >89 slice against the >87 slice of equal size. That is a comparison by QE level, not repetitive vs diverse within one band. The ">87" set may or may not include the >89 pairs (see author_must_check).
- **No mechanism:** they never measure repetition, duplicates or source mix in the >89 slice, so their data cannot separate repetitiveness from source mix. That separation is exactly what C1 asserts.
- **Out-of-domain not established:** they do not report training-data composition, so FLORES cannot be called out-of-domain relative to the top band.
- **Their NMT result is not a counter-example:** removing the bottom ~45% before training from scratch concerns the low tail of the scores, not top-band fine-tuning.

Net effect: the bare phenomenon is pre-empted, while the attribution to repetitiveness is new and untouched by this paper.
notes.relation_to_C2:
**Leaves C2 open.** The evidence is loosely compatible but does not test the claim.

- **Closest result:** at 100k, COMET>87 vs Cleaned gives 35.5 vs 35.7 BLEU and 85.7 vs 85.6 COMET (Table 4). The top band offers no advantage over Cleaned, but it is not clearly worse either.
- **No size-matched control for the >89 slice:** there is no 53k random set. Only the 100k Cleaned set exists, so >89 (33.5) vs Cleaned (35.7) mixes quality with a 53k-vs-100k size difference.
- **"Random" is uncertain:** the paper describes the 100k Cleaned set inconsistently (see author_must_check), so even the 100k comparison may not be top band vs random.
- **Not tested:** no removal of repetition, no vocabulary or word-type statistics. Nothing here bears on "worse than random without repetition" or on vocabulary narrowness.
- **Possible caution:** at the >87 level the LLM showed no penalty against Cleaned, which is weaker than our 0.58 BLEU diverse-vs-random gap. The C2 effect may be smaller, or absent, for LLMs.
notes.how_to_position: In their WMT24 system description, Tan et al. (2024) found that fine-tuning LLaMA2-7B for en->zh on all 53k pairs with a COMETKiwi score above 89 gave 2.6 BLEU less on FLORES than 53k pairs above 87, and that 100k pairs above 87 did no better than 100k sampled pairs. They did not analyse why. We study this effect under controlled conditions, matched in size, length and QE score with multiple seeds, and attribute the out-of-domain loss to the repetitiveness of the selected text rather than to its source mix.
notes.reviewer_risk:
1. **Novelty:** a reviewer can say "Tan et al. (2024) already showed that the highest-QE slice hurts fine-tuning." If our paper presents that phenomenon as new, this citation sinks it. The contribution has to be framed as the controlled attribution (repetitiveness, not source mix) and the random baseline.
2. **Transfer to LLMs:** "Their effect is in a 7B LLM; yours is a small Transformer, so your mechanism may not explain theirs." The LLM arm has to answer this.
3. **Regime:** "Tan et al. show QE filtering clearly helps NMT (+1.4 to +4.4 BLEU), so your negative result only holds in an unusual setting: fine-tuning a converged model at a fixed learning rate on a narrow top band." We must explicitly separate threshold filtering of training data from top-band selection for fine-tuning.
4. **LLM robustness:** their 100k >87 matched their 100k Cleaned set. If our LLM arm shows little or no repetitive-vs-diverse gap, a reviewer will say C1 is specific to small models.
notes.quotes: Sec 5.2: "extremely high QE scores (COMET > 89) even resulted in a decline". I kept only one quote, under 15 words, because this session's copyright rule is stricter than the task's two-quote allowance. Their conclusion in Sec 5.2, paraphrased: improving LLM fine-tuning data quality, at least measured by COMET, is not a promising approach.
notes.author_must_check:
1. **What "100k (Cleaned)" is.** The Table 4 caption calls it random sampling from the Cleaned dataset. The Sec 5.2 text calls it "100k trivial samples (after data cleaning, QE score lower than 80)". The first makes it a random-vs-top comparison, the second a low-vs-top one. Hedge when citing, or ask the authors.
2. **The ">87" sets.** Sec 5.2 says they "lowered the score threshold to 87 and selected another 53k samples". It is unclear whether the 53k >87 set includes the >89 pairs or is drawn only from 87-89.
3. **QE model version for filtering.** Sec 3.1 says only "COMETKiwi model". wmt22-cometkiwi-da is named only for post-editing selection (Sec 3.3), and the introduction says "COMET". COMETKiwi-22 is likely but not stated for filtering.
4. **Full fine-tuning or LoRA** is not stated (Sec 3.2 only says they reuse the ALMA framework).
5. **Inconsistent data sizes in the paper:**
   - The abstract says the LLM was fine-tuned on 100K pairs; Sec 5.2 and Table 3 use 300k.
   - The abstract says the NMT trained on "over 22 million" pairs; the Conclusion says "over 50 million".
   Avoid quoting these sizes.
6. **Numbers I derived, not printed in the paper:** kept fractions of 57%, 55% and 53% (from Table 1); 0.13% and 0.76% of the pool; the -2.6 BLEU / -1.8 COMET gap; the 10k->100k Cleaned gain.
7. **BLEU tokenization.** The SacreBLEU signature in footnote 4 is tok:13a, which is unusual for Chinese output. Do not compare their BLEU magnitudes with zh-tokenized BLEU elsewhere.
8. **Figure 1** (score distributions) is an image, so I relied on the text's statement that about half of en->zh/en->ja scores below 80.
9. **No seeds or variance.** We cannot tell whether the 2.6 BLEU gap exceeds run-to-run noise.
10. **Unknown slice composition.** The paper never lists the corpora in the >89 slice, so whether it is dominated by one source (e.g. UN text) is unknown. Do not claim it is.
11. **Process note:** the PDF and extracted text sit only in this session's temporary scratch folder. Nothing was written to the repository.
notes.useful_for_design:
- **LLM arm, reuse their recipe:** LLaMA2-7B, ALMA's second stage only, lr 2e-5, batch 32 x gradient accumulation 4, 1 epoch, bf16, beam 5 (Sec 3.2). With matching set sizes (53k, 100k, 300k), our numbers can sit directly beside theirs.
- **LLM arm, add the controls they lacked:**
  - a size-matched random set for every top slice (they have no 53k random set)
  - several seeds (they report single runs)
  - test sets beyond FLORES devtest (Table 4 uses only that)
  - COMET (wmt22-comet-da) next to BLEU, because the two diverge in their LLM results. 100k -> 300k at >87 lowers BLEU by 0.9 but raises COMET by 0.9 (Table 4), and LLM fine-tuning trails on BLEU but not COMET (Table 3). Without COMET we invite a "BLEU-only artefact" objection.
- **QE-threshold sweep linking their result to C1:** their damage shows up only at the extreme top (>89, about 0.13% of the pool). At >87 (up to about 0.76%) they see no penalty against their Cleaned set. Our band is about 6%. Measuring rep, duplicate rate and source word types at several depths (e.g. top 0.1%, 1%, 6%) in the en-de pool and the LLM-arm pool would test whether repetitiveness concentrates toward the very top. That would explain their observation with our mechanism.
- **en-de replication:** report the source-corpus composition of the top band (they never do) and keep the E0.5-style matching on size, length, exposure and QE score.
- **Regime control:** if budget allows, add a condition that drops the bottom-scoring half in the en-de or LLM arm. That shows our top-band result does not conflict with the standard finding that QE threshold filtering helps (their Sec 5.1).
- **Vocabulary experiment:** nothing in this paper bears on it directly. Their result that >87 does no better than the Cleaned set at 100k suggests vocabulary narrowness may only hurt at the extreme top, so test the vocabulary-matched control at more than one selection depth.

notes.setup:
IMPORTANT FRAMING: this is mainly a dataset paper about LLM-generated synthetic parallel data (NewsPaLM). QE filtering of a human parallel corpus appears in only ONE baseline row (Table 4 row 1b, plus its extensions in Tables 9 and 12). There is no QE filtering in fine-tuning.
- Language pairs: en->de and de->en only (Sec 3).
- Synthetic data (Sec 2): the source side is Newscrawl 2007-2022 (about 398M English and 507M German lines, Sec 2.1). A subset is chosen by embedding sources with XLM-RoBERTa, clustering them with Recursive Agglomerative Clustering, and sampling uniformly over the clusters (Sec 2.3; cluster counts in Table 1: 3,287 / 3,264 sentence-level, 3,826 / 4,017 blob-level). Targets come from PaLM-2 Bison prompted 5-shot (Sec 2.4), with 512 candidates per source drawn by epsilon sampling (eps = 0.02, Sec 2.4.1). Sentence-level targets are chosen by MBR with a BLEURT utility. Multi-sentence "blobs" of up to 512 tokens are chosen by QE reranking with MetricX-QE (Sec 2.4.2). Greedy-decoded versions are also built as baselines. Sizes (Table 2): MBR sentence-level 998,435 (en-de) and 1,022,344 (de-en); QE blob-level 925,829 and 769,028.
- Human baseline pool (Sec 3.1.1): WMT'23 training data, 296M sentence-level pairs, plus blob-level examples built from about 3M document-bounded sentences (Europarl, News Commentary, Rapid). The paper does not list the other corpora in the pool.
- QE filtering arm (Sec 4.1): BLEURT-QE, following Peter et al. 2023, is applied to the WMT'23 sentence-level data. The top-scoring pairs are kept, sized to exactly match the sentence-level NewsPaLM set ("about one million"). That is about 0.3% of the pool, and the kept set is sentence-level only.
- Models (Sec 3.2): a 602M-parameter Transformer encoder-decoder (Pax) with 8+8 layers, d_model 1024, FFN 8192, 16 heads, no label smoothing, and a 32k bilingual vocabulary trained on WMT'23. The paper uses two regimes. "Pretraining" means training from scratch. "Finetuning" starts from the checkpoint pretrained on all of WMT'23 (Table 6 caption). An LLM arm fine-tunes PaLM-2 Bison on its own MBR/QE outputs (self-distillation) and compares it with 5-shot prompting. The method (full fine-tuning or parameter-efficient) is not stated.
- Training details: steps, learning rate and batch size are not reported. Seeds: none reported; every number appears to be a single run, with no variance or significance tests.
- Dev sets (Sec 3.1.2): newstest2021 (sentence- and paragraph-level) and generalMT2022. The best checkpoint is picked by BLEURT on dev.
- Test sets: WMT'23 for both directions; WMT'24 for en-de only (there is no WMT'24 de-en). The en-de test sets are paragraph-level.
- Metrics (Sec 3.3): MetricX (lower is better), COMET20, COMET22 and BLEURT. They rely mainly on COMET because the MBR data is built with BLEURT and the QE data with MetricX. NO BLEU is reported anywhere.
notes.key_results:
QE filtering, from-scratch pretraining (Table 4, WMT'23 test set; values are MetricX lower-better / COMET22):
- en-de: full WMT'23 (296M) 4.20 / 78.79. BLEURT-QE top ~1M (0.3%) 16.69 / 43.18. NewsPaLM MBR sentence-level, same size 6.39 / 72.05. QE blob-level 2.82 / 80.62. Greedy sentence+blob (9:1) 2.60 / 81.67. MBR+QE (9:1) 2.99 / 79.68.
- de-en: full 5.55 / 82.41. QE-filtered 14.80 / 57.27. MBR sentence-level 4.97 / 80.55. QE blob-level 4.01 / 82.33. Greedy (9:1) 3.47 / 83.30.
- Other metrics (Table 9): BLEURT for the QE-filtered set is 29.33 vs 64.11 for the full set (en-de) and 44.80 vs 69.96 (de-en). COMET20 is -1.14 vs 42.52 (en-de) and -64.27 vs 51.52 (de-en).
- WMT'24 en-de (Table 12): full 3.15 / 77.79 vs QE-filtered 13.06 / 49.38 (MetricX / COMET22).
- Sec 4.1 text: the QE-filtered set "substantially underperforms" NewsPaLM of the same size and also the full WMT'23 set.

Sentence-level vs multi-sentence (Fig 2, Sec 4.1): a model pretrained only on sentence-level data gets worse as segments get longer; the blob-trained model stays flat. The authors conclude that multi-sentence data is essential for paragraph-level test sets.

Fine-tuning from the WMT'23 checkpoint (Table 6, WMT'23 test, COMET22):
- en-de: greedy (9:1) 81.49, MBR sentence-level 82.69, QE blob-level 81.83, MBR+QE 82.52.
- de-en: 84.14, 84.57, 84.27, 84.53.
- PaLM-2 Bison: 5-shot 84.54 rises to 85.64 after MBR fine-tuning (en-de), and 85.36 to 86.26 (de-en).

Curriculum (Table 5): pretraining on greedy data, then fine-tuning on MBR+QE, gives 82.78 (en-de) / 84.05 (de-en). The reverse order gives 81.48 / 83.08.

Data size (Table 16, Sec 4.3.1): a random 25% subsample of the MBR set loses a lot in pretraining (COMET22 72.05 to 59.75 en-de, 80.55 to 75.91 de-en) but little in fine-tuning (82.69 to 82.11, 84.57 to 84.33).

Diversity-aware selection (Table 7, Sec 4.3.2), 25% subsets, uniform over clusters vs following the original Newscrawl distribution, COMET22:
- en-de pretraining 59.75 vs 59.09; en-de fine-tuning 82.11 vs 81.88.
- de-en pretraining is mixed: MetricX 7.41 vs 7.58 favours clusters, COMET22 75.91 vs 76.55 favours the original distribution. de-en fine-tuning 84.33 vs 83.92.
- The authors call the improvement marginal and see "no clear signal" for de-en pretraining.

Per-domain results (Tables 14 and 15; WMT'23: Mastodon, News, Speech, User Review; WMT'24: Literary, News, Social, Speech): NewsPaLM models are strongest on News, but the gains are not limited to News (App. B).
notes.relation_to_C1:
LEAVES C1 OPEN, but partly pre-empts the PHENOMENON.
- What it shows: one independent observation that training on the extreme QE top band of a large web corpus is much worse than the unfiltered corpus (Table 4 row 1b: COMET22 43.18 vs 78.79 en-de, 57.27 vs 82.41 de-en).
- Why it does not establish C1: it says nothing about repetitiveness and nothing about source mix. It never decomposes the top band, and its only explanation is the filtering fraction (0.3%).
- Why it does not contradict C1: our repetitive and diverse halves are the same size and come from the same band, so they share the same fraction. The size/fraction story cannot explain our 2.63-BLEU within-band gap.
- Regime and design differences to state when citing: from-scratch pretraining, not fine-tuning a converged model. BLEURT-QE, not CometKiwi-22. en-de/de-en, not en-fr. A WMT'23 pool of 296M with a 0.3% cut, not 16.6M with about 6%. COMET/MetricX/BLEURT, not BLEU. Single runs, and no in-domain/out-of-domain split.
- The paper also never reports the UN share (or any corpus share) of its filtered set, so it cannot speak to the source-mix confound we control for.
notes.relation_to_C2:
DOES NOT ESTABLISH C2, and does not test it.
- No random-subset baseline: the QE-filtered set is compared only with the full WMT'23 corpus and with NewsPaLM, never with a random 1M sample of WMT'23. So "top band worse than random data of the same size" is not shown here.
- Vocabulary, type counts and lexical diversity of the selected data are never measured.
- The closest related evidence is the diversity-aware sampling ablation (Table 7). It concerns LLM-generated targets, not QE selection. Sampling uniformly over XLM-R clusters gives at most small gains (en-de COMET22 +0.66 in pretraining and +0.23 in fine-tuning; de-en mixed). It is single-run and the authors call it marginal.
- This is weak, indirect support that source diversity matters a little. A reviewer could also read it the other way: diversity effects are small. In size it is comparable to our 0.58-BLEU diverse-vs-random gap.
notes.how_to_position: Finkelstein et al. (2024) observe that keeping only the top 0.3% of the WMT'23 en-de corpus by BLEURT-QE and training from scratch falls far short of using the full corpus (COMET22 43.18 vs 78.79). They suggest the extreme filtering ratio is to blame but do not analyse what the selected subset contains. We study fine-tuning instead and hold size, length, source corpus and QE score fixed: within the QE top band, the damage tracks how repetitive the selected text is, and the band is still worse than random data even without repetition.
notes.reviewer_risk:
1. Novelty: "We already know that aggressive QE top-band selection hurts; Finkelstein et al. 2024 (Table 4) show a collapse." Rebuttal: their observation is from-scratch, single-run and unexplained. Our contribution is the controlled mechanism, in the fine-tuning regime, with 5 seeds.
2. Alternative explanation: "The damage is about the selection ratio or data size, not content." Their only explanation is the fraction. Rebuttal: our two halves have the same size, come from the same band and are length-matched, so the fraction is held fixed. It helps to show this explicitly in a sentence or a small table.
3. Metric choice: their whole evaluation is neural metrics (COMET20/22, MetricX, BLEURT). They warn that data built with a given metric may overfit that metric (Sec 3.3). A reviewer may ask why we report only BLEU, and whether QE-selected data scores differently under COMET. If we add COMET-22, the reviewer may instead raise circularity, since CometKiwi-22 (used for selection) and COMET-22 are closely related. Pre-empt this by reporting a metric unrelated to selection (BLEU or chrF) plus one neural metric, and noting the caveat.
4. Regime: "Fine-tuning is robust to data changes." Their Table 16 shows fine-tuning hardly moves when the data is cut to 25%, while pretraining collapses. A reviewer could argue our fine-tuning effects are small, or specific to a fixed-LR 10k-step schedule. Our 2.6-BLEU gap with t = 33 answers the "small" part, but the schedule-dependence point stands until we check another learning rate or step count.
5. Diversity: a reviewer might cite Table 7 (cluster-uniform sampling gives under 1 COMET22 point) to say diversity or vocabulary effects are minor, which weakens C2.

notes.useful_for_design:
en-de replication:
- Their WMT'23 en-de setup is the natural point of contact. Consider reporting COMET22 (and possibly MetricX) next to BLEU so readers can compare.
- Use the WMT'23 per-domain breakdown (Mastodon, News, Speech, User Review; Table 14) as a cheap out-of-domain probe.
- Beware that WMT'23/24 en-de test sets are paragraph-level. Fine-tuning only on sentence-level data can tank long segments (their Fig 2), which would mix up length and repetitiveness. Use sentence-level test sets (e.g., generalMT2022 or newstest) or report results bucketed by length, and keep our length matching.

Fraction vs content (cheap, no GPU):
- Their explanation is the filtering fraction. We can link their observation to our mechanism by computing the repetitive share and the source-corpus share at several QE cut-offs (e.g., top 0.3%, 1%, 6% of our pool).
- If repetitiveness rises sharply as the cut gets stricter, our mechanism accounts for their fraction effect.
- A short fraction sweep in training, with our random-same-size baseline, would directly answer the "it's just the ratio" objection.

Vocabulary experiment:
- Their cluster-uniform sampling (XLM-R embeddings + agglomerative clustering, Sec 2.3) is a ready "diversity-enforcing" selection to use as a baseline or extra arm next to a vocabulary-matched or vocabulary-expanded arm.
- Their effects were under 1 COMET22 point and single-run, so plan enough seeds to detect differences of about 0.5 BLEU (our diverse-vs-random gap was 0.58).

LLM LoRA arm:
- The paper gives no LoRA or hyperparameter guidance; its LLM fine-tuning is on synthetic MBR data, not QE-filtered human data.
- One takeaway: the LLM gained about 1 COMET22 from about 1M sentence-level in-domain examples (Table 6). Expect small effect sizes in an LLM arm and power it accordingly.
- Their Table 16 suggests fine-tuning is insensitive to set size (25% subsample costs about 0.2-0.6 COMET22). This supports our choice to match sizes (214k-242k) and attribute differences to content.

Evaluation:
- Report at least one metric unrelated to CometKiwi selection (BLEU or chrF) and one neural metric, and state the circularity caveat if COMET-22 is used, as they do in Sec 3.3.

notes.setup:
TASK: the WMT18 Parallel Corpus Filtering shared task. German-English only; no en-fr and no other pair.

POOL: the raw "dirty" ParaCrawl web crawl, which had only minimal deduplication: 104M sentence pairs, about 1B English and 964M German tokens (Sec. 1). It is noisy. In ~300 randomly annotated pairs from their pre-filtered corpus, only 93 were correct translations (Sec. 3.1), which matches the random-scorer precision of 0.312 in Table 1.

INITIAL FILTERING (Sec. 2.1), which cut 104M pairs to 28M:
- dedup after replacing emails and URLs with a placeholder; drop pairs whose source equals the target
- require over 50% of the numbers on each side to have a match
- dedup again after removing all numbers and punctuation
- pyCLD2 language ID: drop if the wrong language is detected with confidence over 0.5
- drop pairs where either side is longer than 150 tokens

SCORING (Sec. 2.2): supervised and MT-based. This is NOT reference-free QE of the CometKiwi kind.
- Main feature, YiSi-1: a Portage phrase-based SMT system trained on the clean WMT18 de-en data translates the German side into English. YiSi-1 then scores that output against the English side, using IDF-weighted bigram lexical similarity over word2vec embeddings, with precision and recall kept as separate features.
- Other features tried:
  - YiSi-2: crosslingual, using bivec bilingual embeddings at unigram level. This is the QE-like variant.
  - SRL variants of YiSi
  - HMM alignment probabilities p(d|e) and p(e|f)
  - sent2vec cosine and Mahalanobis distances
  - perplexity ratio and POS-perplexity ratio
  - 6-gram KenLM perplexities on each side
- A linear L1-regularized regression over all features (Sec. 2.3) was tuned on a synthetic noisy dev set built from WMT09-13 test sets (~11k pairs). It failed and was not submitted.
- Submitted systems: NRC-yisi (YiSi-1 precision only) and NRC-yisi-bicov.

WHAT IS KEPT: the official software takes the top-scored pairs until a 10M-word or a 100M-word budget is filled (Sec. 1, 3.2). The paper gives no pair counts and no pool fraction for these subsets.

"BICOV" REDUNDANCY FILTER (Sec. 2.4): walk down the re-ranked list and drop any pair that adds no new source-language word bigram (a pair of consecutive source tokens) not already seen in earlier pairs. It runs after scoring.

MODELS: all trained FROM SCRATCH on the selected subsets. There is no fine-tuning and no LLM.
- Internal check (Sec. 3.2): Portage SMT, and a Sockeye 1.18.20 Transformer with default settings, max sequence length 60:60 and gradient clipping at 1.
- Official evaluation: SMT and NMT systems trained by the organizers on the submitted selections (Sec. 1, 4).

SEEDS: one run per condition. No variance, confidence intervals or significance tests are reported anywhere.

EVALUATION: BLEU only.
- Internal (Table 2): newstest2017 as dev, newstest2018 as test.
- Official (Table 3): newstest17 as dev; tests are newstest18, iwslt17 (speech), Acquis (law), EMEA (medical), Global Voices (news) and KDE (IT). 48 submissions were ranked.
- Feature sanity check (Table 1): precision among the top 93 pairs of the ~300 annotated ones.
notes.key_results:
FEATURE PRECISION ON THE 300 ANNOTATED PAIRS (Table 1, Sec. 3.1)
- YiSi-1 precision: 0.796 (best)
- YiSi-1 recall: 0.763
- YiSi-2 precision: 0.753
- HMM p(d|e) and p(e|f): 0.753 each
- regression: 0.763
- hunalign: 0.624
- random: 0.312
- Monolingual fluency features are lowest, for example English perplexity 0.355.

INTERNAL BLEU ON newstest2018 (Table 2, Sec. 3.2). Each row gives SMT 10M / SMT 100M / NMT 10M / NMT 100M words.
- random: 20.28 / 26.88 / 24.06 / 34.63
- HMM p(e|f): 23.55 / 29.73 / 26.59 / 39.52
- HMM p(e|f) bicov: 25.31 / 29.98 / 29.08 / 39.66
- YiSi-1 precision (NRC-yisi): 24.68 / 30.10 / 30.75 / 40.27
- YiSi-1 precision bicov (NRC-yisi-bicov): 27.41 / 30.46 / 33.56 / 40.98
- regression bicov: 26.97 / 30.27 / 31.94 / 39.34

So top-scored selections beat random by a wide margin in every condition. For example, NMT 10M is 30.75 vs 24.06 without bicov and 33.56 vs 24.06 with it.

EFFECT OF THE REDUNDANCY FILTER (Sec. 3.2)
- 10M words: +1.61 BLEU for SMT and +2.44 for NMT, "on average". I checked that these equal the mean over the 2 features x {dev, test} in Table 2.
- 100M words: the paper says "virtually no effect". Table 2 actually shows YiSi NMT 100M at +0.73 dev and +0.71 test, and HMM at +0.45 / +0.14.

REGRESSION vs YiSi-1 bicov (Sec. 3.2): the regression was 0.2-0.5 BLEU worse on SMT and 1.6 BLEU worse on NMT.

OFFICIAL RESULTS (Table 3, Sec. 4)
- Averages, NRC-yisi-bicov vs NRC-yisi (rank in brackets):
  - 10M words: 25.65 (8th) vs 25.01 (11th)
  - 100M words: 29.14 (4th) vs 29.07 (5th)
  - overall: 27.39 (6th) vs 27.04 (9th)
  - Best submission overall: 27.90.
- NMT 10M with bicov is better in every test domain:
  - newstest18: 33.93 vs 32.72
  - iwslt17: 24.37 vs 23.89
  - Acquis: 23.20 vs 22.22
  - EMEA: 29.75 vs 28.55
  - Global Voices: 25.44 vs 24.83
  - KDE: 27.75 vs 26.81
  - average: 27.41 vs 26.50, i.e. +0.91
- SMT 10M average: 23.89 vs 23.52.
- Sec. 4 says the official gains from bicov were smaller than in their internal runs.

QUALITATIVE OBSERVATIONS (no numbers given)
- Sec. 2.1: many parallel pairs were similar and uninformative, such as long lists of page numbers or dates. Measures that preferred them gave comparatively poor MT.
- Sec. 2.4: the top-ranked pairs showed much redundancy and limited vocabulary coverage, for example many perfectly translated datelines.
notes.their_explanation:
REDUNDANCY (Sec. 2.4): their scorers reward semantic similarity, not usefulness for MT, so the top of the ranking fills with redundant, low-coverage pairs such as datelines.

NUMBERS AND DATES (Sec. 2.1): measures that preferred numeric lists did poorly, "likely" because the MT systems did not get enough varied data.

HOW MUCH WAS TESTED:
- Only the bicov intervention is tested, as bicov vs no-bicov at a fixed word budget (Tables 2 and 3). The number filters of Sec. 2.1 get no ablation and no numbers.
- The bicov test is a single run per condition with no seeds or significance.
- It does not separate repetition from vocabulary narrowness: one filter acts on both.
- It does not measure redundancy or vocabulary at all: no type counts, no duplicate rates, no n-gram statistics.
- It does not control for domain or source mix.
- Pairs that bicov drops are presumably replaced by lower-scored pairs further down the list, so score level also changes.

OTHER EXPLANATIONS, NONE TESTED:
- Why bicov helps at 10M but hardly at 100M: implied to be because a large selection already has enough coverage.
- Why the official bicov gains were smaller than internal ones: "potentially" differences in MT architecture (Sec. 4).
- Why the 10M-word results were weaker than other top teams: their scorer is good at finding parallel pairs but weaker at ranking usefulness for MT beyond parallelism, so fluency features may help fine-grained ranking (Sec. 4, Sec. 5).
notes.relation_to_C1:
PARTIAL PRECEDENT for the first half of C1 ("top-band selection over-selects repetitive text"). It does NOT establish the causal half, and does not contradict it.

What it shows:
- Sec. 2.4 reports, qualitatively, that the top of a similarity-based ranking is redundant with limited vocabulary.
- Sec. 2.1 reports that preferring numeric or date lists hurt MT.
- Removing redundant pairs at a fixed 10M-word budget raised BLEU (Table 2: NMT +2.44 on average). The NMT gain held across six test domains in the official evaluation (Table 3: +0.48 to +1.21, +0.91 on average).
- This supports the direction "redundancy in the top band costs BLEU, including outside the training domain".

What it does not show:
- Different scorer: an MT-plus-YiSi-1 reference-style score and HMM alignment, not reference-free QE. There are no CometKiwi results.
- Different data: a noisy web-crawl pool with no domain or source labels, not a curated pool.
- Different regime: from-scratch training, not fine-tuning a converged model.
- No quantification of how repetitive the top band is.
- No matched control: dropped pairs are refilled from lower scores.
- One run per condition.
- Nothing about source mix. The "repetitiveness, not source mix" part of C1 is entirely open here, and that disentangling is our contribution.

The "over-selects repetitive text" observation itself is pre-empted at the anecdotal level. We should not present it as new. Our new parts are measuring it for a QE metric and the matched causal test.
notes.relation_to_C2:
Leaves C2 OPEN, and on the surface points the OTHER WAY.

Direction:
- In their setting, top-scored selections are far better than random, even without redundancy removal. Table 2, newstest2018:
  - NMT 10M: 30.75 vs 24.06
  - NMT 100M: 40.27 vs 34.63
  - SMT 10M: 24.68 vs 20.28
- This is not a real contradiction. Their random baseline is drawn from a pool where only about 31% of pairs are parallel (Table 1 random 0.312; Sec. 3.1), so random is crippled by noise. Our pool is curated WMT14 en-fr, and we fine-tune rather than train from scratch.

Vocabulary narrowness:
- Sec. 2.4 names "somewhat limited vocabulary coverage" of the top-ranked sentences as a problem, so they are an early source for the suspect in C2.
- But they lump it together with redundancy. Their bigram-novelty filter targets both at once, and they never test vocabulary independently of repetition.
- The bicov filter only requires one new source bigram per kept pair. That is a different criterion from our rep = 0 (no repeated 8-gram), and it does not make the vocabulary match random's.

So nothing here establishes that a repetition-free top band is still worse than random, or that narrow vocabulary is the cause.
notes.how_to_position:
Draft Related Work sentences:

"In the WMT18 corpus-filtering task, Lo et al. (2018) noted that the pairs their similarity scorer ranked highest were redundant and had limited vocabulary coverage (e.g., repeated datelines). For 10M-word German-English selections, a greedy filter requiring each pair to add a new source bigram raised NMT BLEU by 2.44 on average, but it did little at 100M words. We quantify this redundancy for a reference-free QE metric in a curated pool, separate it from source mix and vocabulary size with matched multi-seed controls, and study fine-tuning rather than from-scratch training."
notes.reviewer_risk:
1. NOVELTY. "That top-scored filtered data is redundant and narrow in vocabulary, and that you need a diversity or coverage step after scoring, has been known since WMT18 (Lo et al. 2018, Sec. 2.4)." The answer has to come from what they did not do: no quantification, no QE metric, no source-mix control, no seeds, no fine-tuning regime. Our abstract must not claim the observation itself as new.

2. MISSING OBVIOUS BASELINE. "Why not apply their bigram-novelty filter to the QE top band and compare with random at matched size?" If top band plus bicov matches or beats random, C2 weakens, and the practical message becomes "use a known fix".

3. DIRECTION OF C2. "Lo et al. find top-scored data beats random by 5.6-6.7 BLEU (Table 2), so your 'worse than random' must come from your regime (fine-tuning a converged model at a fixed LR, a clean pool)." We have to explain why random is a strong baseline in a curated pool and a weak one in ParaCrawl.

4. SIZE DEPENDENCE. "Their redundancy effect is large at 10M words and near zero at 100M (Tables 2 and 3). Your 1M-pair band may sit in a size range where redundancy happens to matter." This means a selection-size sweep, or at least a discussion.

Apply the Sec. 2.4 bigram-novelty filter ("bicov") to the CometKiwi top band at our matched size, length and exposure, and compare with random UN and with our rep = 0 half.    - For out-of-domain claims, their official multi-domain test sets (iwslt17, Acquis, EMEA, Global Voices, KDE, alongside newstest) are a good template.
