notes.setup:
A system description for the WMT19 parallel corpus filtering shared task (low-resource track). This is not a controlled study.
- Language pairs: Nepali-English and Sinhala-English (Sec. 1). Hindi data is used only to train the scorer.
- Pool: the noisy test corpora crawled from the web for ParaCrawl (Sec. 1). This paper never gives the pool size.
- Scoring: each pair gets its own score, from one of three scorers.
  - YiSi-2 (Sec. 2.2.1) is a reference-free, "bilingual" semantic quality metric. It averages idf-weighted cosine similarity of cross-lingual word embeddings over unigrams, with alpha = 0.5. The embeddings come in two versions:
    - "sup": bivec trained on the provided parallel data. That is 563k pairs of IT and religious text for ne-en and 647k pairs of IT and subtitles for si-en (Table 1).
    - "unsup": vecmap applied to w2v. Wikipedia on the ne/si side, news (779M sentences) on the English side, with 9k/8k dictionary pairs (Table 1).
  - XLM (Sec. 2.2.2) is a Transformer pretrained with cross-lingual language-model training and then fine-tuned to classify sentence pairs as good or bad. This follows the Zipporah approach. Negatives are made by four corruption procedures at 1 positive to 4 negatives. The model has 6 layers and 512-dimensional embeddings. Pretraining ran only about 16 hours, with batch 32 and lr 2e-4. Fine-tuning used batch 8 and lr 1e-5. Training data was about 1B tokens with 80K BPE merges and a vocabulary of 95,056 (Sec. 2.2.2, Table 2).
  - Ensemble: a rank-average of the scorers (Sec. 2.4).
- Pipeline (Sec. 2):
  1. Pre-filtering (Sec. 2.1). Remove duplicates after masking emails, URLs and numbers. Remove most pairs with number mismatches, pairs in the wrong language (pyCLD2), pairs with more than 150 tokens on either side, and pairs where over 50% of the ne/si side is English, numbers or punctuation.
  2. Scoring, as above.
  3. Re-ranking for vocabulary coverage (Sec. 2.3). Walking down the ranked list, a pair loses 20% of its score if it adds no source-side word bigram unseen in the higher-ranked pairs.
- What is kept: the organizers' script takes the top-ranked pairs until a sample of 1M words or 5M words is reached (Sec. 1, 3.2). The paper does not say which side the words are counted on.
- Models: everything is trained from scratch, with no fine-tuning and no LLMs.
  - In development, the authors trained Portage phrase-based SMT on the 1M and 5M samples (Sec. 3.2).
  - The official test results use the organizers' SMT and NMT systems. The NMT architecture is not described in this paper (Sec. 4).
- Seeds: not reported. Every number is a single run.
- Evaluation: BLEU on Wikipedia translation test sets (Guzman et al. 2019). Development used uncased BLEU on the official dev-test set (Table 4), and the official results are on the test sets (Table 5). Table 3 also reports how accurately the XLM classifier separates real pairs from generated negatives.
notes.key_results:
- Classifier accuracy (Table 3, Sec. 3.1): with confounders drawn from the test set and fine-tuned on classification only, accuracy is 96.3 (hi-en), 99.3 (ne-en), 94.8 (si-en), average 96.8. Adding masked-LM training during fine-tuning lowers it to an average of 93.1. With confounders drawn from the training set: 94.8 (classification only) and 92.8 (with masked LM). Footnote 9: always guessing "negative" scores 80%.
- Scorer domain bias (Sec. 3.1): the XLM model scores most pairs in the test corpora below 0.5. Its top-scoring ne-en pairs contain a lot of biblical text, which the authors read as domain bias inherited from the Bible-heavy ne-en fine-tuning data. This is a qualitative inspection only, with no counts.
- Dev-test BLEU, SMT, uncased, ne-en 1M / 5M | si-en 1M / 5M (Table 4):
  - random: 1.30 / 3.01 | 1.43 / 3.33. This baseline still had pre-filtering and the coverage re-ranking applied (Sec. 3.2).
  - Zipporah (their re-run): 4.14 / 4.42 | 4.12 / 4.96
  - YiSi-2-sup: 3.86 / 3.76 | 4.85 / 4.71
  - YiSi-2-unsup: 4.42 / 3.91 | 3.97 / 4.56
  - XLM-v2-spc: 4.14 / 4.09 | 4.52 / 4.72
  - ensemble: 3.94 / 3.95 | 4.89 / 4.85
  - Every scored system beats random by roughly 1-3 BLEU. For several systems the 5M sample is no better, or worse, than the 1M sample (Sec. 3.2).
- Official test BLEU, rank in brackets, out of 21 submissions (ne-en) and 23 (si-en), in the order SMT-1M / SMT-5M / NMT-1M / NMT-5M (Table 5):
  - ne-en ensemble: 4.10 (3) / 4.30 (8) / 4.58 (5) / 1.10 (14)
  - ne-en XLM-v2-spc: 3.92 (7) / 4.51 (4) / 4.03 (7) / 1.40 (9)
  - si-en YiSi-2-sup: 3.87 (6) / 4.39 (9) / 4.97 (3) / 1.58 (9)
  - si-en ensemble: 4.19 (3) / 4.54 (4) / 4.06 (4) / 1.39 (11)
- Summary (Sec. 4): the ensemble was best in 4 of the 8 test settings, with an average of 3.53. For NMT, BLEU collapses going from 1M to 5M words in every system, for example ne-en ensemble 4.58 to 1.10 (Table 5).
- No ablation: there is no result with versus without the vocabulary-coverage re-ranking. Its effect on BLEU is never measured.
notes.their_explanation:
- Redundancy and narrow vocabulary (Sec. 2, 2.3): the authors assume a good training corpus needs high source-vocabulary coverage and varied sentence lengths, for robustness (Sec. 2, bullet list). They note that scoring each pair independently produces redundant top-ranked sets with limited source-word coverage, and they add the bigram-novelty penalty to counter this (Sec. 2.3). This is stated as motivation and never tested. There is no ablation, and the re-ranking is even applied to the random baseline.
- Biblical text at the top (Sec. 3.1): they attribute it to domain bias from the scorer's Bible-heavy fine-tuning data. This rests on brief inspection only.
- NMT collapse at 5M words (Sec. 4): they suggest the test corpora contain fewer than 5M words of data clean enough for NMT, so larger samples pull in noise. They also suggest SMT tolerates noise better. Neither explanation is tested.
- Conclusion (Sec. 5): they say more experiments are needed to understand why small top-ranked samples work but larger ones do not. They also say a better way to re-rank for vocabulary coverage might improve MT. Both are left as future work.
notes.relation_to_C1:
The paper anticipates part of C1 but leaves its causal core open.

What it anticipates: it says plainly that per-pair scorers yield top-ranked sets with redundancy and limited source vocabulary (Sec. 2.3), and it builds a fix into its pipeline. So the observation that top-band selection favours repetitive text has a 2019 precedent. The precedent is qualitative, uses a different scorer (YiSi-2 and an XLM classifier, not CometKiwi), and covers web-crawled low-resource ne/si-en data. C1 should therefore not be framed as discovering the redundancy.

What it does not establish:
- (a) It never measures how repetitive the top band is.
- (b) It never measures what that repetitiveness costs in BLEU. The re-ranking is not ablated.
- (c) It never separates out-of-domain from in-domain effects.
- (d) It never separates repetitiveness from source mix.

On (d), its one observation about composition, biblical text at the top for ne-en (Sec. 3.1), is exactly the source-mix confound that C1 controls for. The paper attributes it to domain bias and does not disentangle it.

Nothing in the paper contradicts C1. Our E0.5 result is new against it: a gap of 2.63 BLEU inside UN-only text, matched on size, length, pretraining exposure and QE score. The setting also differs (fine-tuning a converged model, not training from scratch).
notes.relation_to_C2:
The paper leaves C2 open and gives no evidence on it.

1. Its random baseline loses to every scored selection by about 1-3 BLEU (Table 4: random 1.30-3.33 vs scored 3.69-4.96). On the surface that points the opposite way from "the top band is worse than random". The settings are not comparable, though:
   - their pool is noisy web crawl, so random picks up garbage, while ours is a pre-scored pool where random UN text is clean;
   - they train from scratch at 1M or 5M words, while we fine-tune a converged model;
   - their "random" still had pre-filtering and coverage re-ranking applied (Sec. 3.2).
   So the paper does not contradict C2. A reviewer could still cite Table 4 naively.
2. On mechanism, the paper shares C2's prior: vocabulary coverage matters (Sec. 2, 2.3, 5). It never tests this. There is no coverage ablation, no type counts, and no comparison of vocabulary narrowness across subsets.
3. Its NMT drop from 1M to 5M words (Table 5) is put down to noise, not vocabulary, and is untested.

Overall: C2's vocabulary-narrowness hypothesis is plausible enough to have been built into a 2019 system, but it is still unverified. That leaves room for our vocabulary experiment.
notes.how_to_position: Suggested Related Work sentence: "Bernier-Colborne and Lo (2019) observed that scoring each sentence pair on its own yields redundant top-ranked sets with limited source vocabulary, and countered this with a bigram-novelty re-ranking whose effect they did not measure. We quantify this redundancy for a modern QE metric (CometKiwi). Holding source mix, length, pretraining exposure and QE score fixed, we show it accounts for a 2.6 BLEU out-of-domain loss when fine-tuning on the top band."
notes.reviewer_risk:
Main objection: "It has been known since WMT19 that per-pair scorers give redundant, low-coverage top sets (Bernier-Colborne & Lo 2019, Sec. 2.3). Filtering systems already re-rank for coverage. The contribution is incremental, and the paper omits the obvious baseline: a coverage or bigram-novelty re-ranking of the QE top band."

Secondary objections a reviewer could raise from this paper:
1. Random sampling was far worse than scored selection in WMT filtering (Table 4), so C2's "worse than random" looks like an artefact of a clean, pre-filtered pool or of the fine-tuning regime. We must explain why our random UN baseline is a fair comparison.
2. Scorer domain bias is known: their top ne-en pairs were biblical, following the scorer's training data (Sec. 3.1). So the 77% UN skew in our top band is expected, and the novelty rests entirely on the within-UN control in E0.5.

notes.author_must_check:
1. Pool size of the ne-en and si-en test corpora. This paper does not give it; take it from the WMT19 filtering-task findings paper (Koehn et al. 2019). I report no number for it.
2. The official NMT and SMT systems used for Table 5 are not described here; they are the organizers' systems. Check the findings paper before describing the training regime as "from scratch" in detail.
3. Whether the 1M/5M-word budget counts English-side words. This paper only says "samples containing 1M or 5M words" (Sec. 1).
4. Table 4 values are dev-test BLEU from the authors' own Portage SMT runs. The "Zipporah*" row (ne-en 3.40/4.22, si-en 4.16/4.77) was reported by the organizers with a different SMT setup. Do not mix these with Table 5.
5. Ranks in Table 5 marked "T-" are ties, for example "4.07 (T-14)".
6. YiSi-2 is called a quality-estimation metric, but it is an embedding-similarity metric, not a trained QE model like CometKiwi. Be careful calling this "QE filtering" in our Related Work.
7. The 20% coverage penalty uses source word bigrams; our "rep" statistic uses 8-grams within the band. These are related but different statistics.
8. The XLM scorer was undertrained (about 16 hours of pretraining, Sec. 2.2.2). Any comparison to our scorer quality should be hedged.
9. All results are single runs with no seeds or variance, and many differences between systems are 0.1-0.5 BLEU at absolute levels of 1-5 BLEU.

notes.setup:
THIS IS NOT A QE-FILTERING PAPER. It studies catastrophic forgetting, meaning the loss of generic quality when a pretrained NMT model is fine-tuned on one domain, and asks which properties of the fine-tuning set predict that loss.
- Language pairs: German->English (de-en, into English) and English->Japanese (en-ja) (Sec 2.2, App. A).
- Pretraining (App. A): one from-scratch Transformer per pair, built with the Tensor2Tensor toolkit. de-en is trained on 43.9M lines (Paracrawl v9, Europarl v10, NewsCommentary v14, Tilde, WikiMatrix); en-ja on 22.4M lines of JParacrawl v3.0. Table 11: deep encoder and shallow decoder (de-en 15 encoder / 3 decoder layers, en-ja 18/3). The table prints "hidden 2560, filter 640". BPE: 32K shared merges for de-en, 16K unshared for en-ja. Each model is pretrained only once, on 4 GPUs for about 2 days.
- Fine-tuning data (Table 1, Sec 2.2). These are whole domain corpora; nothing is selected or scored.
  - de-en: the five OPUS multi-domain sets from Aharoni & Goldberg 2020: IT 223K, Koran 18K, Law 467K, Medical 248K, Subtitles 500K (size-capped).
  - en-ja: IWSLT 220K, KFTT 427K, BSD 20K.
  - Generic baseline scores: de-en 35.3 BLEU / 0.54 COMET; en-ja 22.5 / 0.43 (Table 1).
- Training: every fine-tuning run is fixed at 20K steps (Sec 2.2), about 1 GPU-hour each (App. A). The paper gives no learning rate, optimizer or batch size for fine-tuning.
- Seeds: none reported. Every number is a single run from a single pretrained model, and there are no variance estimates or significance tests between systems. The only statistics are Kendall's tau correlations across domains.
- Evaluation:
  - Generic test set: concatenated WMT News/General test sets, 2019-22 for de-en (5,769 segments) and 2020-22 for en-ja (4,037) (Sec 2.2, Table 1). Plus each domain's in-domain test set.
  - Metrics: BLEU (SacreBLEU v2.0; Mecab tokenizer for ja), COMET (wmt20-comet-da, fn 3), and a new token-level score, ForgetGenUse (Sec 2.1, Eq 1). For each reference token, ForgetGenUse counts how often the original model produced it correctly and the adapted model no longer does. It can be split into tokens that appear in the adaptation set (ID) and tokens that do not (OOD).
- Variables they manipulate:
  - Size subsampling to Koran/BSD token counts (Table 5).
  - Shortest-segment subsampling, plus a LASER-filtered variant with cutoff 0.8 (Table 6).
  - Corpus-level heuristics (Table 7): NLL under the generic model, vocabulary JSD, and source/target vocabulary coverage. Coverage is the share of the generic subword vocabulary that appears at all in the domain set.
  - Mix-in intervention (Sec 4, Tables 8-10): Random 1:1 (as many random generic lines as in-domain lines) vs "Minimal Mix-in". Minimal Mix-in adds a generic line only if it contains a target token not yet in the adaptation set, which brings target coverage to 100%.
notes.key_results:
1. Fine-tuning loss differs widely by domain (Table 2: drop on generic test sets after 20K steps).
   - BLEU drop: IT 5.0, Koran 22.3, Law 4.7, Medical 8.3, Subtitles 5.7; IWSLT 4.8, KFTT 2.0, BSD 7.0.
   - COMET drop: 0.11, 0.78, 0.08, 0.16, 0.09; 0.07, 0.06, 0.29.
   - ForgetGenUse_All: 0.09, 0.25, 0.07, 0.11, 0.09; 0.14, 0.11, 0.16.
   - BLEU and COMET drops correlate across domains (Kendall tau = 0.8, p < 0.05). ForgetGenUse correlates significantly with neither (Sec 2.2).
2. Tokens absent from the fine-tuning set are lost far more often (Table 4).
   - ForgetGenUse_OOD: 0.37, 0.60, 0.27, 0.47, 0.11; 0.34, 0.65, 0.49.
   - ForgetGenUse_ID: 0.07, 0.17, 0.07, 0.09, 0.09; 0.14, 0.11, 0.12.
   - Lost tokens are replaced by tokens that occur in the adaptation set, even where the source has nothing in-domain. Examples: billion -> million, week -> month, Trump -> Donald, England -> United Kingdom (Table 3, Sec 2.3).
3. Dataset size does not explain it (Sec 3.1, Table 5).
   - Size has no significant tau with the BLEU or COMET drop. ForgetGenUse shows tau = 0.7, p < 0.05, described as a negative correlation with size.
   - After subsampling every domain to Koran's token count, drops are still uneven: BLEU IT-s 10.4, Koran 22.3, Law-s 12.3, Med-s 14.4, Sub-s 11.5.
4. Very short segments and noisy pairs accelerate loss (Table 6).
   - Law: shortest-segment subset (Law-ss, 17.0 tokens average) drops 12.4 BLEU, about the same as the random Law subset (Law-s, 12.3).
   - Subtitles: shortest-segment subset (Sub-ss, 12.5 tokens) drops 30.4 BLEU / 1.27 COMET, against 11.5 for the random subset.
   - LASER-filtering Sub-ss (Sub-ssf) cuts the drop to 15.1 BLEU.
   - LASER-filtering Koran changes little: 0.3 BLEU worse, 0.01 COMET better, ForgetGenUse unchanged. Their conclusion is that quality alone does not explain forgetting.
5. Of the dataset heuristics, only coverage tracks forgetting (Table 7, Sec 3.3).
   - NLL under the generic model: weak correlation with the BLEU drop only (tau = 0.5, p < 0.1).
   - Vocabulary JSD: no significant tau with any of the three forgetting measures.
   - Target coverage: IT 0.52, Koran 0.23, Law 0.59, Med 0.48, Sub 0.62; IWSLT 0.62, KFTT 0.72, BSD 0.29.
   - Coverage vs COMET drop: tau = 0.6 (source) / 0.9 (target), p < 0.05, inverse.
   - Coverage vs BLEU drop: tau = 0.7 for target (p < 0.05), 0.6 for source (p < 0.1).
   - ForgetGenUse: significant only with source coverage (tau = 0.7).
   - Adding the subsampled domains (coverage 0.34-0.52) gives "significant and strong" correlation with all metrics. No tau is printed for this.
6. Filling the vocabulary gaps recovers most of the loss (Sec 4.1, Tables 8-9).
   - Minimal Mix-in adds 8.5K-22.8K generic lines, under 10% of the in-domain size except for Koran and BSD (Table 8).
   - Mean BLEU drop: de-en 9.2 with no mix-in, 1.5 with Random 1:1, 2.2 with Minimal Mix-in; en-ja 4.6 / 0.4 / 1.7.
   - Mean COMET drop: de-en 0.24 / 0.02 / 0.05.
   - Minimal Mix-in is within 1 BLEU of Random 1:1 for 6 domains and within 0.03 COMET for 7.
   - It recovers at least 80% of Random 1:1's mitigation for 6 domains (BLEU) and 4 domains (COMET).
   - It works worst for Subtitles and IWSLT, which already had high coverage.
7. In-domain gains survive (Table 10, in-domain test sets).
   - Mean de-en BLEU gain: 5.8 with no mix-in, 4.6 with Random 1:1, 5.6 with Minimal Mix-in.
   - For Koran, mixing in generic data raises in-domain BLEU: 5.3 with none vs 6.1 / 6.4.
notes.their_explanation:
Mechanism they propose (Secs 2.3-2.4, 3.3, 4.1, 5): fine-tuning moves the model's lexical choices toward the target vocabulary of the adaptation set. Generic tokens that never appear in that set get replaced by plausible tokens that do, often in contexts with no in-domain trigger. The amount and kind of forgetting therefore depends on how much of the generic (subword) vocabulary the adaptation data covers, with target-side coverage the strongest correlate.

They link this to Gu & Feng 2020 (decoder embeddings track preserved generic performance) and suggest future work on decoder embeddings for tokens missing from the in-domain data. That part is not tested.

What they test:
(a) Correlation across 8 domains, single runs (Table 7), after ruling out sentence count, NLL and vocabulary JSD.
(b) One intervention, Minimal Mix-in, which raises target coverage to 100% and largely removes forgetting (Table 9).

Gaps in their test:
- No same-size random mix-in control. Minimal Mix-in adds about 9-23K lines and is compared only with no mix-in and with Random 1:1, which is 10-50x larger. So the benefit of covering the vocabulary is not separated from the benefit of adding a little generic data.
- Coverage is never varied with domain held fixed.
- No seeds.
- Only mid-sized from-scratch Transformers; LLMs are explicitly left for future work (Limitations).

Secondary explanations:
- Very short segments, and misaligned short pairs, accelerate forgetting (Sec 3.2, partly tested by LASER filtering).
- Small amounts of noise do little harm (Sec 3.2).
notes.relation_to_C1:
C1 is LEFT OPEN: the paper neither establishes nor contradicts it, and it contains a competing explanation.
- It never uses QE scores, data selection, source mix or n-gram repetitiveness. The only nod to repetition is a hypothetical in the Introduction (a 1,000-sentence sample vs 1,000 copies of one sentence pair), which is never run.
- Our "out-of-domain damage" on newstest2014 is the same thing they call forgetting on generic test sets, so C1 is a claim about that phenomenon.

The competing explanation: forgetting tracks the vocabulary coverage of the fine-tuning set. In our data the repetitive half has the narrowest vocabulary: 25,134 source word types vs 33,874 for the diverse half at equal word count, plus an 8.45% duplicate rate. E0.5 matched size, length, pretraining exposure, QE score and source mix, but NOT vocabulary coverage. Under their account, the 2.63-BLEU repetitive-vs-diverse gap could be a coverage effect, with repetitiveness only standing in for it.

What does hold up against this paper:
- "not source mix" (they say nothing about source mix).
- Matching on pretraining exposure: their NLL-under-generic-model heuristic barely predicted forgetting, which makes it plausible as a matched nuisance variable rather than the cause.

Wording C1 as "repetitiveness, as opposed to vocabulary coverage, drives the damage" is not supported by our data, and a reader of this paper would ask for that separation.
notes.relation_to_C2:
C2 is SUPPORTED AS A HYPOTHESIS, NOT ESTABLISHED, and its novelty is pre-empted.
- This paper is the main prior evidence that a fine-tuning set's vocabulary coverage predicts generic-quality loss: target coverage vs COMET drop tau = 0.9 across 8 domains (Table 7), and a coverage-filling mix-in that removes most of the loss (Table 9).
- So "vocabulary narrowness is the leading suspect" is consistent with their results and should be credited to them, not presented as our idea.

It does not establish C2 for QE-selected data:
- It never compares a selected subset with random data from the same pool or domain.
- Its evidence is correlation across domains that differ in many ways, with n = 8 and one run each, plus an intervention without a same-size random control.
- Our E0.5 is a cleaner setting: same domain (UN text), same size and length, diverse vs random UN at 33,874 vs 58,441 types, 0.58 BLEU difference, 5 seeds.

Where our data departs from their framework: on the in-domain UN test set the diverse half is -2.11 vs baseline while random UN is +0.20. In their Table 10, in-domain fine-tuning always improves in-domain scores. Coverage of generic vocabulary does not obviously explain an in-domain loss, so if C2 is meant to cover the in-domain result as well, it needs its own argument.
notes.how_to_position: Saunders and DeNeefe (2024) show that catastrophic forgetting in NMT domain adaptation tracks the target vocabulary coverage of the adaptation set across eight domains, and that a small coverage-completing generic mix-in recovers most of it. We study the same failure inside a single domain, where QE top-band selection, matched on size, length, QE score and pretraining exposure, yields a narrower vocabulary than random data. We test whether n-gram repetitiveness hurts beyond what reduced coverage explains. (Keep that last sentence only if the vocabulary experiment actually separates the two; otherwise present coverage as their hypothesis and our results as consistent with it.)
notes.reviewer_risk:
Main objection: "Saunders & DeNeefe (2024) already showed that forgetting during fine-tuning is driven by the adaptation set's vocabulary coverage. Your repetitive half has the fewest word types (25,134 vs 33,874 vs 58,441), so both C1 and C2 reduce to that known mechanism. 'Repetitiveness' is a proxy for low coverage, and the only new finding is that QE top-band selection lowers coverage."

Our E0.5 matches many confounds but not coverage, so we cannot rebut this yet.

Secondary objections a reviewer could build from this paper:
(i) We report only BLEU, and they show BLEU and COMET miss harmful vocabulary shift (ForgetGenUse does not correlate with either, Sec 2.2). Expect requests for COMET and a token-level analysis.
(ii) A single newstest2014 set is a narrow "generic" test; they concatenate four years of WMT test sets for reliability and topic spread (Sec 2.2).
(iii) Any coverage intervention we run must include a same-size random-data control. Their own design lacks one, and a reviewer who knows the paper may check that we do not repeat the gap.
notes.quotes: Abstract: "the amount and type of forgetting is linked to that data's target vocabulary coverage". This is the only quote I am giving, because a stricter limit than the task's (one quote under 15 words) applies to me. The second-best line, from the opening of Section 3, says in substance that many domain features do not correlate with forgetting while vocabulary coverage does. That is a paraphrase, not a quote.
notes.author_must_check:
1. Seeds and variance: I found no mention of multiple seeds or variance anywhere in the text or appendix (only "a fine-tuning run" and one pretraining run per pair). Confirm before writing that they used a single seed.
2. Fine-tuning hyperparameters: no learning rate, optimizer or batch size is given (Appendix A covers architecture, data and steps only).
3. Kendall tau sample size: the text says correlations are "across the sets of domains". I could not tell whether the 5 de-en and 3 en-ja domains are pooled (n = 8) or analysed per pair. With n = 5-8, p < 0.05 needs a large tau, and p < 0.1 counts as "weakly significant".
4. Sec 3.1 prints tau = 0.7 for ForgetGenUse vs dataset size and calls it a "negative correlation". The sign is not shown, so quote it as printed.
5. No tau value is printed for the "significant and strong correlation" once the subsampled domains are added (end of Sec 3.3).
6. Table 11 reads hidden size 2560, filter size 640. This looks swapped relative to usual Transformer conventions; reproduce it as printed if cited.
7. The de-en BLEU tokenization signature is not given (only SacreBLEU v2.0, plus Mecab for ja).
8. Their coverage is the share of the generic model's SUBWORD vocabulary that appears at least once, computed separately for source and target. Our descriptive statistic is source WORD types at equal word count. The two are not directly comparable; compute their measure before claiming agreement.
9. I did not check whether an arXiv version differs from the Anthology PDF, or whether supplementary material exists beyond Appendix A.
10. Pang et al. 2024 (arXiv:2401.08350), cited in their Limitations as finding similar terminology forgetting in LLMs fine-tuned on the same OPUS de-en domains: I only saw their one-sentence description, not the paper.
notes.useful_for_design:
Vocabulary experiment:
1. Use their coverage definition, which reviewers will know: the share of the pretraining subword vocabulary that appears at least once in the fine-tuning set, computed separately for source and TARGET (target was the strongest correlate, tau = 0.9 with the COMET drop). Compute it now for repetitive, diverse and random UN. This is descriptive and needs no GPU.
2. Design the intervention to separate repetitiveness from coverage, which is what C1 needs.
   (a) A Minimal-Mix-in-style top-up: add the few UN rows that contribute uncovered target tokens, to both the diverse and the repetitive half. Include a same-size top-up of random UN rows as the control; this is the control they lacked.
   (b) Alternatively, or additionally, build subsets from the same pool matched on size, length and QE score that differ only in coverage (greedy max vs min), and repetitive subsets with coverage matched to the diverse half. If repetitive still loses after coverage is matched, C1 holds as stated.
3. A separate duplicate-removal control for the repetitive half (8.45% duplicate sources), so that exact duplication is not confused with n-gram repetition.

Free analysis on existing outputs: compute ForgetGenUse_ID/OOD (Sec 2.1, Eq 1) on the E0.5 newstest2014 translations already produced. The coverage hypothesis predicts higher out-of-vocabulary token forgetting for the diverse and repetitive halves than for random UN. Also add COMET for every arm, since they show BLEU hides harmful vocabulary shift.

Test set: consider adding a concatenated multi-year WMT generic test set alongside newstest2014, as they did, for reliability.

Segment length: short and misaligned segments sharply accelerate forgetting (Sub-ss 30.4 BLEU drop). Keep the length-histogram matching in the en-de replication, and check that the en-de QE top band is not enriched for very short pairs.

LLM LoRA arm: they leave LLMs untested and point to Pang et al. 2024 for similar terminology forgetting in LLMs. Read Pang et al. before fixing the LoRA design. Whether a LoRA-tuned LLM shows the same coverage and repetitiveness sensitivity is an open gap we could claim.

Compute and strength: they fix steps (20K) to isolate data effects, the same logic as our fixed 10K steps. They use one run per condition; our 5-seed design is a methodological advantage worth stating.

notes.setup:
LANGUAGE PAIRS: en<->de, en<->ja, en<->zh, both directions (6 directions) (Sec. 4). No en-fr.
DATA / POOL: the full WMT training data as released by the organizers, which the authors note is already cleaned (Sec. 4). Table 3 sizes (full / kept 50% / kept by both BleurtQE and Bicleaner): de<->en 292.8M / 146M / 105M; en<->zh 55.2M / 27.6M / 17.5M; en<->ja 33.9M / 16.9M / 10.4M. All pools include ParaCrawl; en<->zh includes about 19.7M back-translated Chinese sentences (Table 3 caption). The paper does not break the pools down by source corpus and does not report the corpus mix of the kept half.
SCORING: four conditions. (1) Random half. (2) Bicleaner AI, a noise-detection classifier (Sec. 4.1.2). (3) CometKiwi (Sec. 4.1.3). (4) BleurtQE, their own reference-free BLEURT-style metric on a modified mT5, trained on WMT DA 2015-2020 (Sec. 3). On WMT'22 MQM, segment-level Pearson r / Kendall tau (Table 1): en-de BleurtQE 0.38/0.29 vs CometKiwi 0.43/0.29; en-ru 0.41/0.39 vs 0.39/0.36; zh-en 0.38/0.35 vs 0.51/0.36. Pairs are scored in the en->X direction only, and that score is reused for both training directions (Sec. 4.1.3).
WHAT IS KEPT: the top 50% by score, set by a threshold (Sec. 4.2). The 50% was 'chosen in preliminary experiments on the English to German data' and those experiments are not reported (Sec. 4). Only this one fraction is tested.
MODEL: a Transformer encoder-decoder (PaxML) trained from scratch on each selection. 6+6 layers, d_model 1024, FFN 8192, 16 heads, gated GELU, 32k shared vocabulary per pair, max 128 tokens, 551M parameters. Trained 'until they converged'. The checkpoint is picked by BLEURT on WMT'22, which therefore acts as the dev set (Sec. 4.2). There is no fine-tuning and no LLM.
SEEDS: none mentioned; it appears to be one training run per condition. Significance uses a pairwise permutation test (Koehn 2004) at p=0.05, which covers test-set variance only, and 'Random' is left out of the significance computation (Table 2 caption).
EVALUATION: COMET22 is the primary metric. They chose it over BLEURT to avoid overfitting, because BleurtQE is BLEURT-based (Sec. 4.2). BLEURT, BLEU and chrF are given in Appendix B.2 (Tables 13-18). Test sets (Sec. 4.3): WMT'19 (news, where available), WMT'22 (also the dev set), WMT'23, IWSLT'21 (TED) and the IWSLT'23 dev set (ACL talks, a technical domain). Test segments over 128 tokens were dropped, which cut WMT'23 en->de from 557 to 404 and de->en from 549 to 468 (Table 6). Per-domain WMT results are in Tables 7-12.
notes.key_results:
All numbers are COMET22 from Table 2 unless another table is named.
1) Halving the data at random hurts. en->de WMT'23: None 81.8, Random 80.8 (the text says 'by 1 point', Sec. 4.4).
2) The QE half beats both full data and the random half on most cells.
- en->de: BleurtQE / CometKiwi / None / Random = 87.2 / 86.9 / 86.2 / 84.0 (WMT'22 dev); 86.7 / 86.7 / 86.0 / 85.5 (WMT'19); 83.5 / 82.9 / 81.8 / 80.8 (WMT'23; the '+1.7' in Sec. 4.4); 83.9 / 83.6 / 83.2 / 82.8 (IWSLT'21); 85.1 / 84.8 / 84.5 / 84.2 (IWSLT'23).
- de->en WMT'23: both QE metrics 84.6 vs None 83.3 (+1.3).
- en<->ja: largest gain +2.3 on WMT'23 (ja->en BleurtQE 78.2 vs 75.9). Footnote 8 mentions +2.4 on WMT'22 but discounts it because WMT'22 is the dev set.
- en<->zh: up to +2.8 on WMT'23 (en->zh CometKiwi 82.5 vs 79.7).
3) Against the random half in COMET22, both QE metrics score at or above Random in every cell of Table 2 (6 directions x 3-5 test sets). The smallest margin is 0.1 (de->en IWSLT'23: 87.3 vs 87.2).
4) The out-of-domain sets are where the gains stop (Sec. 4.4, Table 2):
- IWSLT'23 shows little or no gain for several directions.
- ja->en IWSLT'23: None 85.5 beats CometKiwi 85.0 and BleurtQE 85.1.
- zh->en IWSLT'23: None 84.9 vs CometKiwi 84.5.
- en->zh IWSLT'23: None 84.2 vs QE 84.1.
- de->en IWSLT'23: None 87.4 vs QE 87.3.
- In BLEU (Table 17), every way of halving the data loses about 4.6-5.2 BLEU on en->zh IWSLT'23 (None 52.5; Random 47.6; Bicleaner 47.9; CometKiwi 47.9; BleurtQE 47.3).
5) BLEU sometimes disagrees with COMET22 (Appendix B.2), and some QE cells fall below Random in BLEU. The authors do not discuss any of these:
- en->de WMT'19, BleurtQE: BLEU 42.1 vs None 43.1 and Random 42.4, while COMET22 is 86.7 vs 86.0 (Table 14).
- zh->en IWSLT'23, CometKiwi: BLEU 30.8 vs Random 31.7 and chrF 61.6 vs 62.1 (Table 18).
- en->zh IWSLT'23, BleurtQE: BLEU 47.3 vs Random 47.6 (Table 17).
6) Sentence length: at 50% the QE selection made sentences slightly longer, from 14.4 to 15.5 words per sentence for BleurtQE on en<->de. The authors contrast this with Koehn et al. (2020) on shorter sentences (end of Sec. 4.4).
7) Per-domain results (Appendix B.1, Tables 7-12): gains hold across domains. Full data beats BleurtQE in only two cases: de->en ecommerce 85.4 vs 85.3 (Table 8) and zh->en manuals 77.7 vs 77.5 (Table 10).
8) BleurtQE and Bicleaner agree on only about two thirds of the kept sentences (Table 3, Sec. 5). Using the intersection (about one third of the data) does worse than BleurtQE alone: -0.3 BLEURT en->de and -0.6 BLEURT de->en on WMT'22 (Sec. 5.3).
9) Synthetic noise, en->de, 200K examples per category, threshold at the median (Table 5). Share kept as valid, BleurtQE vs Bicleaner: misaligned 8.1 vs 5.6; misordered src 24.3 vs 39.1; misordered tgt 10.3 vs 6.3; wrong language 43.8 vs 0.0; untranslated src 47.6 vs 0.0; untranslated tgt 63.8 vs 0.0; overtranslation 35.2 vs 13.9; undertranslation 13.4 vs 7.5.
notes.their_explanation:
Their reading: QE metrics are trained to pick up fine-grained quality differences, so they keep the best translations instead of only removing obvious noise (Sec. 1, Sec. 6). From hand inspection of de-en only (Sec. 5.1, Table 4), BleurtQE removes four kinds of pairs that Bicleaner keeps:
(a) 'Single entity mistranslations' in templated text. These are sentence pairs built on a common template ('Flights from cityA to cityB', 'Hotels in city') where the entity or number differs between the two sides.
(b) Low-quality or unnatural language on both sides.
(c) Pairs that are related but misaligned.
(d) Bible and similar religious text, which they guess is removed because of archaic language.
Bicleaner is much better at gross noise: wrong language and untranslated text (Table 5).
HOW FAR THIS IS TESTED: only partly. The categories come from qualitative inspection, and footnote 10 says they could not produce exact statistics for each effect. Sec. 5.1 says they used automatic clustering (after Aharoni and Goldberg, 2020) to look at topic distribution, but no clustering result appears in the paper. The noise behaviour is tested on synthetic data (Table 5). Nothing links any of the categories causally to the BLEU or COMET gains: there are no ablations, no breakdown of the kept half by domain or source corpus, and no analysis of repetition, duplicates or vocabulary. The Bible and archaic-language explanation is offered with 'probably' and is not tested. Limitations: tuning the threshold per method could have done better but would cost too much, and starting from raw crawled data would allow a deeper comparison.
notes.relation_to_C2:
AT FACE VALUE CONTRADICTS an unscoped C2. In their setting, QE-selected data is never worse than random data in COMET22: both QE metrics score at or above Random in every cell of Table 2, with margins from 0.1 to over 3 points. Caveats:
- Random was excluded from their significance tests.
- They ran one training run per condition.
- A few BLEU and chrF cells in the appendix put a QE half below Random, which the authors never mention. CometKiwi zh->en IWSLT'23: BLEU 30.8 vs 31.7, chrF 61.6 vs 62.1 (Table 18). BleurtQE en->de WMT'19: BLEU 42.1 vs 42.4 (Table 14). BleurtQE en->zh IWSLT'23: BLEU 47.3 vs 47.6 (Table 17). These are anecdotal and are not support for C2.
Our C2 is a different and more controlled comparison: the rep=0 half of an extreme top band vs random text inside UN text only, matched on size, length, pretraining exposure and QE score, with 5 seeds, for fine-tuning. Peter et al. do not test that regime. On mechanism, they say nothing about vocabulary breadth, type counts or lexical diversity, so the vocabulary-narrowness hypothesis is fully open. Bottom line: no support for C2. It must be worded as 'the extreme QE top band, used for fine-tuning', not 'QE-selected data', or Table 2 will be cited against it.
notes.how_to_position: Peter et al. (2023) show that keeping the QE-best half of the WMT training data (CometKiwi or BleurtQE) and training from scratch beats both the full data and a random half in COMET22 for en<->de/ja/zh. We study a different part of the ranking and a different regime: fine-tuning a converged en-fr model on only the extreme top of a CometKiwi-22 ranking (about 1M of 16.6M pairs). There the selected text is dominated by repetitive material, and this repetitiveness, rather than source mix, drives the out-of-domain loss. The two findings can both hold if the benefit of QE selection depends on how far down the ranking one keeps.
notes.reviewer_risk:
The likely objection: 'Peter et al. (2023) found that QE filtering consistently beats random selection and full data across six directions and several domains, including out-of-domain IWSLT. Your negative result is an artifact of your setup.' The reviewer could point to five features:
(i) An extreme threshold: about 6% kept vs their 50%. They also say per-method threshold tuning would help (Limitations).
(ii) Fine-tuning a small converged Transformer-base for a fixed 10k steps instead of training to convergence.
(iii) BLEU-only evaluation. They explicitly favour neural metrics (Sec. 4.2), and their own appendix shows QE filtering can lower BLEU while raising COMET22: en->de WMT'19 BleurtQE has BLEU 42.1 vs None 43.1 with COMET22 86.7 vs 86.0 (Table 14). A reviewer may say our BLEU losses are a metric artifact.
(iv) A single, UN-heavy en-fr pool.
(v) Use of CometKiwi, which correlated better than BleurtQE on 2 of 3 pairs in their Table 1, yet BleurtQE was their stronger filter on several sets. The reviewer may argue the conclusions depend on which QE metric is used.
Our partial defences: 5 seeds against their single runs; a size-, length- and QE-matched random UN baseline; a pre-registered design. These only answer (ii) to (iv) if we add COMET or another neural metric and the en-de replication, and (i) needs a selection-fraction sweep.
notes.quotes: "sentences that have a common structure, but that differ in one or few components" (Sec. 5.1, 'Single Entity Mistranslations' paragraph, p. 567). This is their description of templated texts, which they say are abundant in WMT de-en training data. Only one quote is given; other passages are paraphrased.
notes.author_must_check:
1) Which CometKiwi checkpoint they used. Sec. 4.1.3 footnotes the OpenKiwi URL and cites Kepler et al. (2019); Table 1 and Related Work cite Rei et al. (2022). The exact model (for example wmt22-cometkiwi-da) is never named. Do not write 'the same metric as ours' without verifying.
2) The source-corpus mix of their pools and kept halves is not reported. Whether the WMT zh-en data they used includes UN text, and so could have shown a UN-heavy top half, cannot be answered from this paper. Check the WMT'23 data page separately before saying anything about it.
3) Seeds and number of runs are never stated. I read this as one run per condition, but the paper never says so explicitly.
4) The fraction study behind the 50% choice ('preliminary experiments' on en->de, Sec. 4) is not reported, so the paper has no evidence about the top 5-10%.
5) The topic clustering mentioned in Sec. 5.1 has no reported results.
6) Small inconsistencies in the paper. The Sec. 4.4 summary says that except for 'English -> Japanese' QE does not hurt on IWSLT'23, but Table 2b shows the drop in ja->en (en->ja improves). Table 9 labels its rows 'COMET22' and 'BLEURT' where CometKiwi and BleurtQE seem to be meant. The bolding in Table 17's IWSLT'23 chrF column looks wrong: Bicleaner 42.3 is bold while None is 47.1. Do not cite those specific cells without care.
7) Their BLEU and chrF tokenization for zh and ja is not stated.
8) The length shift from 14.4 to 15.5 words is reported only for BleurtQE on en<->de.
notes.useful_for_design:
1) Selection-fraction sweep, which bridges our regime to theirs. Compute rep share, duplicate source rate and UN share for the top 50%, 25%, 12% and about 6% of the CometKiwi ranking. If budget allows, add one fine-tuning run per fraction. This answers the 'Peter et al. kept 50% and it helped' objection head-on. It is cheap for the descriptive part.
2) en-de replication: score in the training direction. Peter et al. scored en->X only and reused the score for both directions (Sec. 4.1.3), which they admit is a bias.
3) en-de replication: repetition may look different. Their de-en evidence is web templates such as 'Flights from X to Y' and 'Hotels in city', common in travel, finance and technical text. Many are shorter than 8 tokens, and their mean sentence length is about 14-15 words. An exact 8-gram rep statistic gives rep=0 to any source under 8 tokens and can miss slot-varied templates. Before the en-de run:
- check how rep handles short rows;
- consider an added template measure (rep with entities and numbers masked, or a shorter n);
- report the share of rows too short to score.
4) Keep length matching. QE selection shifted length even at 50% (14.4 to 15.5 words, Sec. 4.4).
5) Measure and match corpus composition of the en-de top band, as in E0.5. Their Bible observation shows QE selection is correlated with text type.
6) Metrics. Add COMET22, their primary metric, so results are comparable. Because we select with CometKiwi (COMET family), also report a non-COMET metric such as chrF plus BLEURT or MetricX. This mirrors their own reason for not evaluating BleurtQE-filtered systems with BLEURT (Sec. 4.2).
7) Out-of-domain sets. For the en-de arm, WMT'23 en->de and IWSLT TED or ACL-talk sets would line up with their Table 2a. Note they truncated WMT'23 at 128 tokens (557 to 404 segments).
8) Keep 5 seeds and significance tests against Random. They had neither for Random, and this is our clearest methodological advantage.
9) LLM LoRA arm: the paper has nothing on LLMs or fine-tuning, so there is no design input and also no prior result to conflict with.
10) Vocabulary experiment: the paper has no lexical analysis. One detail: their 32k vocabulary is built per language pair, and it is not stated whether it was rebuilt on the filtered data. For us the base vocabulary is fixed, so the experiment should target word-type coverage, not subword inventory.

notes.setup:
Structure: Intro, Related Work, Task (S3), Data (S4), Evaluation Protocol (S5), Results (S6), Methods used by Participants (S7). There is no conclusion and no limitations section; the paper ends after S7 and the acknowledgements.
- Language pair: German-English only. Translation direction: the SMT 5-gram LM is "trained on the English side of the subset" (S5.3), so English is the target (de->en). The paper never states the NMT direction separately.
- Pool: about 1 billion English words of very noisy web-crawled Paracrawl data, "deduplicated from a subset of the raw Paracrawl Release 1" (S3, S4.1). The pool size in sentence pairs is NOT given in this paper. Released per pair: the EN sentence, the DE sentence, a Hunalign score and the source URLs (S4.2). The organisers' cursory inspection (Table 1) rates only 23% of pairs as okay and 41% as misaligned.
- Scoring: there is no single scoring or QE metric. 17 teams submitted 44 score files with one arbitrary score per pair, where higher means better (S3, S5.1). Methods (S7) are typically pre-filter rules (length, length ratio, language ID, number/URL mismatch, near-copies), then scoring functions (n-gram or neural LMs on clean data, LMs on the raw data as contrast, NMT models, bag-of-words lexical translation probabilities), then a classifier trained on good pairs vs synthesised or raw bad pairs. Nothing like CometKiwi exists here (2018).
- What is kept: the top-scored subset at a fixed size counted in ENGLISH WORDS. The official sizes are 10M words (about 1%) and 100M words (about 10%) (abstract, S3). The organisers threshold on the score and randomly include tied pairs at the threshold to hit the size (S5.2). They count English rather than German words so that a submission cannot select pairs with few German words (S5.2). After the deadline they also trained on 20, 30, 50, 80, 150 and 200M words for a handful of systems (S6.3, Fig. 1-2).
- Models: everything is trained FROM SCRATCH on the selected subset. There is no fine-tuning and no LLM. SMT is Moses with basic settings and a 5-gram LM on the subset's English side only (S5.3). NMT is Marian v1.5 defaults with 50k BPE, max length 100, "dropout of 0.2 for RNN states" (so an RNN model, though the architecture is not named), beam 12 with length normalisation, 20 epochs (about 10h) for 10M and 10 epochs (about 2 days) for 100M (S5.3).
- Seeds: none reported. Each subset appears to be trained once, and no variance is given.
- Baselines: there is NO random-selection baseline and NO unfiltered or full-pool baseline in any table.
- Evaluation: case-insensitive BLEU with multi-bleu-detok.perl (S5.3). The official score is the average BLEU over 6 test sets (S4.3, Table 2): newstest2018 (2,998 sents), IWSLT 2017 TED (1,138), Acquis EU law (2,862), EMEA medical (3,000), GlobalVoices (3,000) and KDE software localisation (3,000). Acquis and KDE keep only 15-80-word sentences and EMEA only 20-80. All three are deduplicated, and all test sets were checked for overlap with the pool; a PHP-docs set was dropped because it was inside Paracrawl (S4.3). Dev sets were newstest2016 and newstest2017 (S3). The task explicitly targets quality, not domain: news-relevance subsampling was discouraged and the undisclosed test sets get more weight (S3).
notes.key_results:
All numbers are average BLEU over the 6 test sets unless stated otherwise.
- Best scores (S6.1, Table 4): NMT 10M 28.6 (microsoft), NMT 100M 32.1 (microsoft), SMT 10M 24.6 (rwth-nn-redundant), SMT 100M 26.5 (microsoft). NMT beats SMT at both sizes. The authors note that SMT normally relies on large monolingual LMs (S6.1).
- How much the scorer matters depends on the cut (S6.1). At 10M only 2 submissions are within 0.5 BLEU of the best for SMT and 0 for NMT. At 100M, 15 are within 0.5 for SMT and 9 for NMT. Scores differ more at 10M than at 100M, and more for NMT than for SMT.
- Spread across submissions, NMT 10M (Table 4): 6.6 (utfpr-forest) to 28.6. Excluding UTFPR the lowest is 13.5 (afrl-cvg-small). NMT 100M: 6.2 to 32.1.
- Per domain (S6.2, Tables 5-6): the authors see no system doing better on some domains "more than random variance would lead to expect". The one exception they name is rwth-nn and rwth-nn-redundant at 10M, which do much better on newstest, GlobalVoices and IWSLT relative to others. Column order in Table 6 was checked against PDF coordinates (Avg, newstest, IWSLT, Acquis, EMEA, GV, KDE).
- Domain skews that are in Table 6 but not discussed in the text (NMT 10M):
  - lmu-ds-lm-si: newstest 31.2 but Acquis 16.8 and KDE 14.7 (avg 22.1).
  - afrl-cvg-large: newstest 11.2, IWSLT 6.1, EMEA 23.8 (avg 13.8).
  - microsoft: 35.7 / 25.1 / 23.7 / 32.7 / 26.7 / 27.8.
- Size curves (S6.3, Fig. 1-2): NMT curves for the high-performing systems "peak almost always at 100 million words", occasionally at 80 or 150. Scores collapse at 150 and 200M because some participants gave almost all remaining pairs the same low value. SMT curves are flatter, with several systems inside a 1-BLEU band from 30 to 200M words (Fig. 2 caption). The authors cannot tell whether 100M is optimal for this corpus or whether participants overfitted to it, though they guess the former.
- Pool noise (Table 1, S4.1): okay 23%, misaligned 41%, third language 3%, both English 10%, both German 10%, untranslated 4%, short segments of up to 2 tokens 1% and of 3-5 tokens 5%, non-linguistic characters 2%.
- Variants whose names suggest redundancy or diversity handling (Table 4; the variants are not described in this paper):
  - alibaba vs alibaba-div: identical in all four columns (24.1 / 26.4 / 27.6 / 31.9).
  - rwth-nn vs rwth-nn-redundant: differ by at most 0.1 BLEU.
  - vicomtech vs vicomtech-ngsat ("n-gram saturation" per the Azpeitia et al. title): NMT 10M 26.4 vs 25.6, NMT 100M 30.4 vs 24.9 (-5.5); SMT within 0.1.
notes.their_explanation:
The paper gives very little causal explanation, and nothing it suggests is tested.
(1) Noise is especially harmful for NMT. This motivates the task and is cited to Khayrallah & Koehn 2018 (S1); it is not re-tested here.
(2) NMT beats SMT. Their account is that SMT normally relies on large monolingual LMs, which this setup withholds (S6.1). This is an assertion.
(3) The NMT peak at 100M words is "just an optimal value for this corpus" rather than participants overfitting to the announced size. This is stated as a guess, and they say they cannot tell (S6.3).
(4) The collapse at 150 and 200M is a scoring artefact: participants gave the same low value to everything outside their 100M (S6.3). This is an observation about the submissions, not an experiment.
(5) They leave open whether near-boilerplate "okay" pairs (untranslated names, numbers, web navigation strings) help or hurt (S4.1).
They do not explain why the 1% cut separates methods more than the 10% cut. They do not analyse what any selected subset contains: no domain, vocabulary, duplicate or repetition statistics. They also do not explain the per-test-set skews visible in Table 6.
notes.relation_to_C1:
LEAVES C1 OPEN. It neither establishes nor contradicts the claim.
- Nothing in the paper measures repetitiveness, n-gram redundancy, source mix or the domain make-up of the selected subsets, and no subset is ever split by any property.
- The setting differs on every axis that matters for C1:
  - de-en noisy web crawl, not a curated en-fr pool;
  - 44 heterogeneous scorers, not one QE model;
  - from-scratch RNN/SMT training, not fine-tuning a converged Transformer;
  - single runs.
Indirect points that touch C1:
(a) The pool was deduplicated before release (S4.1), so exact-duplicate pairs never reached the scorers. Our repetitive half still has an 8.45% duplicate-source rate, so the WMT18 protocol would have removed part of what we call repetitive.
(b) The authors' reading of the six-domain results is that selections did not specialise by domain beyond random variance (S6.2). That is a qualitative claim with no test. Table 6 still shows large selection-specific domain skews at the 1% cut (lmu-ds-lm-si: newstest 31.2 vs KDE 14.7), which the paper does not explain. So the paper does not support "QE selection is domain-neutral", but it also says nothing about why skews arise.
(c) Variants named -div, -redundant and -ngsat exist, but this paper does not describe them. Their table differences (0.0, at most 0.1, and -0.8 / -5.5 for NMT) cannot be read as evidence for or against repetition effects without reading the system papers.
notes.relation_to_C2:
LEAVES C2 OPEN.
- The paper contains no random-selection baseline at any size, so it cannot speak to "top band worse than random".
- It contains no vocabulary analysis: no type counts, coverage or OOV figures.
- The only size-related evidence is the curve shape (S6.3, Fig. 1): NMT on the top-ranked subset improves from 10M to about 100M words and then falls. Size and ranking depth move together there, so this does not bear on a fixed-size comparison like ours.
Possibly relevant but unverifiable from this paper: the AFRL "cvg" systems (Erdmann & Gwinnup 2018, "Coverage and cynicism"). The name suggests coverage-driven selection, which could be vocabulary coverage. afrl-cvg-large and afrl-cvg-small score 13.8 and 13.5 on NMT 10M, against 27.1 for afrl-cvg-mix-meteor (Table 4). If "cvg" is vocabulary coverage, a pure coverage selector did badly here, which would bear on how we frame the vocabulary hypothesis. This must be checked in the AFRL system paper before citing it either way.
notes.how_to_position: "The WMT 2018 parallel corpus filtering task (Koehn et al., 2018) fixed the now-standard protocol of scoring a noisy pool, keeping the top-scored 1% or 10% by word count, and training MT on the result across six domains; it found that scorers diverge most at the tight cut but did not examine what the selected subsets contain or compare them with random selection. We study exactly that: the content of a QE-selected top band, against size-, length- and score-matched random controls, in a fine-tuning setting."
notes.reviewer_risk:
1. Exact-duplicate confound. "Deduplicating the pool before selection is standard practice since WMT18 (S4.1). Your repetitive half has an 8.45% duplicate-source rate, so the effect may simply be undeduplicated data." To pre-empt this, show that the repetitive-vs-diverse gap survives after removing exact and near-duplicate sources, or report it on a deduplicated repetitive half with size and length re-matched.
2. Domain-shift objection. "WMT18 separated quality from domain relevance and evaluated on six domains (S3, S6.2). Your out-of-domain damage after fine-tuning on 77% UN text is ordinary domain shift, not a property of QE selection." E0.5's UN-only, matched design answers this for source mix, but the paper must say so explicitly. It should also report more than one out-of-domain test set, since newstest alone is a single domain. WMT18 averaged six.
3. Setting mismatch. "Filtering findings are about from-scratch training on noisy crawl; fine-tuning a converged model on 214k pairs at a fixed learning rate is a different question." Our framing must state up front that we study fine-tuning, not corpus construction.
4. Prior redundancy-aware selection. A reviewer may point to the WMT18 variants named -div, -redundant and -ngsat and to AFRL coverage selection as prior work on redundancy, diversity or coverage in filtering. We need to read those system papers so we are not claiming novelty they already have. Minor point: WMT18 ran single runs with no variance, so our 5-seed design is a strength, not a risk.
notes.quotes:
I give one direct quote instead of the two the brief allows, to stay within the quotation limit I work under. The second point is paraphrased.
1. S4.1, p. 728, on pairs counted as okay that are mostly untranslated names, numbers or web navigation strings: "if such data is also harmful, merely irrelevant, or maybe even beneficial", which the authors call an open question.
2. Paraphrase, S3, p. 727: the task addresses data quality, not domain-relatedness. Participants were discouraged from subsampling for news relevance, and the undisclosed test sets are weighted more.
notes.author_must_check:
1. The pool size in sentence pairs is not stated anywhere in this paper; only "1 billion words (English token count)" is. Get the pair count from the task website or a system paper. Do not cite one from memory.
2. Translation direction: de->en is inferred from the SMT LM being trained on the English side (S5.3). It is not stated outright for NMT.
3. The NMT architecture is only "default settings of version 1.5" with RNN-state dropout. The paper never names it, so do not call it a Transformer.
4. S6.3 says results were computed for "six systems", but the Fig. 1 and Fig. 2 legends list seven (alibaba, arc-13, microsoft, nrc-yisi-bicov, prompsit-lm, rwth-nn, rwth-nn-redundant). Cite "a handful of top systems" or check.
5. This paper does not describe what alibaba-div, rwth-nn-redundant, vicomtech-ngsat or afrl-cvg-* do. Read these before citing them in connection with C1 or C2:
   - Lu et al. 2018 (Alibaba)
   - Rossenbach et al. 2018 (RWTH)
   - Azpeitia et al. 2018 (Vicomtech, "n-gram saturation")
   - Erdmann & Gwinnup 2018 (AFRL, "Coverage and cynicism")
6. The per-test-set numbers I quote from Table 6 were checked for column order against PDF coordinates (Avg, newstest2018, IWSLT2017, Acquis, EMEA, GlobalVoices, KDE). Re-check against the PDF if you cite a specific cell.
7. The "within 0.5 BLEU" counts (S6.1) are the authors' own counts and were not recomputed. They note that many come from the same participants.
notes.useful_for_design:
- Deduplication arm (affects C1 robustness, all arms). WMT18 deduplicated the pool before anyone scored it (S4.1). Add a control that removes exact (and ideally near-) duplicate sources from the repetitive half, then re-matches size and length. Also report the gap before and after. This directly pre-empts reviewer risk 1.
- Multi-domain evaluation for en-de. WMT18 provides a ready-made de-en multi-domain test suite: newstest2018, IWSLT17, Acquis, EMEA, GlobalVoices, KDE (S4.3, Table 2). For the en-de replication, use several out-of-domain sets rather than newstest alone, and report per-set as well as averaged scores. Check direction: newstest2018 mixes both original directions (S4.3), and the other sets would need reversing for en->de.
- Test/pool overlap check. WMT18 dropped a test set because it was inside the pool (S4.3). Run the same overlap check between our in-domain UN test set and the 16.6M pool, and especially the repetitive half. Boilerplate overlap could inflate or distort the in-domain numbers (+0.20 / -2.11 / -2.65).
- Size by words, not pairs. WMT18 matched subset sizes by target-side English word count to stop length gaming (S5.2). Keep matching by tokens (not just pair count and length histogram) in the en-de and LLM-LoRA arms, where tokenizers differ.
- Ties at the threshold. WMT18 broke score ties randomly at the cut (S5.2). With CometKiwi top-band scores packed into 0.896-0.914, check score precision and ties at the band edge, and fix the tie-break with a seed.
- Cut depth for the vocabulary experiment. Method differences were far larger at the 1% cut than at the 10% cut (S6.1). Consider running the vocabulary experiment and the random comparison at two or more band depths (e.g. top 1M vs a looser band). This shows whether C2's "worse than random" shrinks as the band widens, which separates narrowness from selection depth.
- Random baseline as a contribution. WMT18 never reports random selection. Our random-UN control (31.17) is something this line of work lacks, so state it explicitly in the paper.
- Reading list before designing the vocabulary arm: AFRL "Coverage and cynicism" (coverage-driven selection) and Vicomtech "n-gram saturation". If either already selects for vocabulary breadth or penalises n-gram redundancy, reuse its definition as a baseline in the vocabulary experiment rather than inventing a new one.

notes.setup:
- **Language pair:** Japanese<->English, both directions.
- **Training pool:** KFTT (Kyoto Free Translation Task: Japanese Wikipedia articles about Kyoto, professionally translated). Table I gives 440,288 pairs; Sec IV-A says "approximately 440,000". The pool is single-source and single-domain.
- **Preprocessing (Sec IV-A):** Unicode NFC normalisation; removal of misaligned and empty segments; MeCab for Japanese; deduplication; removal of pairs with "excessive repetition or non-language tokens"; lowercasing; truncation to 512 tokens. No thresholds are given, and the pool size after filtering is not reported.
- **Selectors (Sec IV-C):**
  - Random: a uniform sample.
  - Top-TF-IDF: mean TF-IDF of the sentence.
  - Top-FD-Score: geometric distance from the TF-IDF centroid, used as a diversity selector.
  - Top-QuRate: the QuRate-1.3B model, which scores writing clarity, factuality and educational value.
  - Top-COMET-Kiwi: reference-free QE; per Sec III-C, the top-k by COMET-Kiwi score. The checkpoint is not named. The text cites the CometKiwi WMT22 QE submission (ref [9]; the in-text numbering is off by one or two throughout).
  - The paper does not say which language side TF-IDF is computed on.
- **What is kept:** top-k, with k = 10,000 in the main runs (Tables III and IV) and k = 1,000 in an ablation that compares only TF-IDF and COMET-Kiwi (Table II). That is about 2.3% and 0.23% of the 440,288 pool (my arithmetic; the paper gives no fraction). All subsets have the same number of examples. Sec IV-A also says "identical token sizes", but no token counts are given. Selection is not length-matched.
- **Models (Sec IV-B):** four 7B LLMs described as instruction-tuned: LLaMA-7B, Gemma-7B, Qwen2-7B and Mistral-7B. Exact checkpoints are not given, and the Qwen citation points to the Qwen3 report. Models are loaded in 8-bit and fine-tuned with LoRA; LoRA rank and alpha are not given.
- **Hyperparameters (Sec IV-B):** learning rate 2e-4; 1 epoch; batch size 2 with gradient accumulation 8, so about 625 steps (Fig. 4's x-axis ends near 620); maximum length 512; AdamW with 5% linear warmup; FP16. The hardware is stated as "NVIDIA A400". No model is trained from scratch.
- **Seeds:** a single seed (42). There are no variances, confidence intervals or significance tests.
- **Evaluation:** a "WMT24 Japanese-English" test set of 998 pairs (Table I), used for both directions, scored with BLEU and COMET. Neither the BLEU implementation, its Japanese tokenisation nor the COMET model is specified. The Introduction promises in-domain KFTT test results, but none are reported; only WMT24 numbers appear. A 2,000-pair held-out validation set is listed in Table I.

notes.their_explanation:
The authors credit COMET-Kiwi's "semantic awareness": it weighs adequacy and meaning over surface lexical overlap (Sec III-C, V-F d).
- **Qualitative claim (Sec V-E, Tables VI and VII):** pairs only COMET-Kiwi picks are well-formed, self-contained explanatory sentences. They also expose the model to "diverse domains (religion, public health, nutrition, mathematics, everyday products)".
- **Training loss (Sec V-G):** the smoother, lower loss means the model "encounters fewer noisy or inconsistent training pairs". Because the curves look alike across architectures, they argue the gains come from the data distribution rather than the model.
- **Conclusion (Sec VI):** "data quality, not data quantity" drives low-resource LLM fine-tuning.

**Is this tested? No.** The support is descriptive only: the uniqueness counts, 5+5 hand-picked examples, a box plot of output COMET, and loss curves. There is:
- no ablation of length, domain, repetition or vocabulary;
- no matching of subsets on any property besides example count;
- no second seed and no significance test.

Two further points:
- The authors never consider that low training loss could mean easier, shorter or more predictable text rather than better text.
- Their diversity claim rests on five examples. Three of the five "best" COMET-Kiwi-only pairs in Table VI are about Buddhism or funerals.

My reading of Fig. 3 seems to contradict their variance claim. TF-IDF has the narrowest box (about 0.76–0.80), and COMET-Kiwi has the widest interquartile range (about 0.735–0.855). The text says semantic selectors show "markedly narrower variance" than TF-IDF.
notes.relation_to_C1:
**Leaves C1 open. It neither establishes nor contradicts it.**
- The paper never measures whether the QE-selected set is repetitive or what sources it comes from, and the pool has only one source.
- Repetition was filtered out before any scoring: Sec IV-A removes duplicates and pairs with "excessive repetition". That most likely means within-sentence repetition and exact duplicates, not the cross-corpus shared 8-grams our rep statistic captures. Either way, their design suppresses the phenomenon C1 is about rather than testing it.
- Nothing in the paper separates repetitiveness from source mix or domain. KFTT is all Kyoto Wikipedia, so there is no source mix to separate.

The only tangential hint is anecdotal. Table VII's lowest-ranked COMET-Kiwi picks include list-like fragments (e.g. "4 – Mugi fishing port (Tokushima Prefecture)"), which fits QE scoring formulaic short text highly. Do not cite it as evidence.

The inferred overlap of at least 6,700 pairs between the TF-IDF and COMET-Kiwi top-10k (my arithmetic from Table V) hints that their COMET-Kiwi selection lines up with a surface lexical feature, possibly sentence length. The paper does not discuss this.
notes.relation_to_C2:
**On the surface the paper reports the opposite of C2. It does not test C2's mechanism.**

The headline result: COMET-Kiwi top-10k beats a same-size random sample out of domain (WMT24) in BLEU in 8 of 8 model-direction cells and in COMET in 6 of 8 (Tables III and IV). This comes from a pool already deduplicated and filtered for repetition. That is the closest published thing to "top QE without repetition beats random", the reverse of C2.

It is not a clean counter-example:
1. **Different regime:** 7B LLMs with LoRA for one epoch (~625 steps), against our converged from-scratch Transformer-base fine-tuned for 10k steps.
2. **Different pool:** a single-domain pool of 440k pairs, top ~2.3%, with no UN-like institutional text, against our 16.6M multi-source pool and top ~6%.
3. **No matching:** QE and random are not matched on length, tokens or vocabulary. COMET-Kiwi likely favours short pairs, which also fits the much lower training loss in Fig. 4.
4. **Single seed:** swings between selectors reach about 10 BLEU (Gemma JA->EN: TF-IDF 10.09 vs COMET-Kiwi 20.25), and COMET disagrees with BLEU in several cells.
5. **Data-integrity problems** in the tables (see author_must_check).

**Vocabulary narrowness is not examined.** Table I gives type counts for one unattributed "Selected Subset (10k)", so it cannot show whether COMET-Kiwi picks a narrower vocabulary than random. The C2 vocabulary hypothesis stays fully open.
notes.how_to_position: Fujita de Mello and Takada (2025) compare five selectors for LoRA fine-tuning of 7B LLMs on Japanese–English (KFTT, 10k of 440k pairs, one seed). They find that COMET-Kiwi top-k beats random selection on WMT24, but their pool is single-domain and deduplicated and filtered for repetition before scoring, and they do not analyse what the selected data looks like. We work with a 16.6M-pair multi-source pool in which the QE top band is dominated by repetitive text, and use controls matched on length, size, QE score and source with five seeds to show that this repetitiveness, not source mix, drives the out-of-domain loss, and that even the non-repetitive part of the band falls below matched random data.
notes.reviewer_risk:
**Likely objection:** "Fujita de Mello & Takada (IEEE BigData 2025) show COMET-Kiwi top-k selection beating random for LLM fine-tuning in every BLEU comparison. Your negative result (C2, and the damage in C1) may be specific to an old from-scratch Transformer and a UN-heavy pool. It may also go away once standard dedup and repetition filtering, which they apply, is done before QE ranking."

**Answer:**
- Ours is a different regime, and the planned LLM LoRA arm tests it directly.
- Their comparison is single-seed and not length-matched, and their tables have internal inconsistencies.
- Exact dedup would not remove our phenomenon. The repetitive half has only an 8.45% duplicate-source rate, and rep > 0 is about shared 8-grams, not exact copies. That is our number, so please confirm it backs this argument.

**Secondary risk:** a reviewer may point to their within-sentence "excessive repetition" filter and ask whether our rep statistic just captures what any normal cleaning pipeline removes. We should state precisely how rep differs from within-sentence repetition and from exact duplicates.
